items.title: xtouch-daemon
items.text: xtouch-daemon turns a Behringer X-Touch Extender into a hardware mixer for PipeWire on Linux. Its motor faders, LED meters and scribble strips control your devices and applications. A strip can also belong to Home Assistant instead, for lights, speakers in other rooms or scenes.

items.title: Strips
items.text:
• Device strips (output, input) control an output or an input, or whatever is the default. Select makes the device the default, and its LED shows which one is. See Devices.
  • Several devices on one strip: a list or a * wildcard (e.g. bluez_output.* for any Bluetooth headphones). The strip shows the one that is there, and Select switches between them.
  • Sound card profiles: Rec switches the card between profiles, e.g. analog and digital output. The label of the active profile names the strip, and each profile can have its own volume range.
  • Application strips (apps) control all streams of a group of applications at once, e.g. every browser. A stream that starts later gets the strip's volume. See Applications.
  • Auto strips (auto) pick up the next application that plays and has no strip of its own. They keep it for a few seconds after it stops, so it does not jump between strips from track to track. The encoder picks another application, a push pins it. Aliases give applications readable names.
  • Home Assistant strips (homeassistant) turn a strip into entities for your automations over MQTT discovery: the motor fader, the encoder, the LCD lines and color, the LEDs, and events for every button press. See Home Assistant.
  • Empty strips (empty) stay dark and do nothing.

items.title: On every strip
items.text:
• Motor faders glide to new values smoothly, follow changes made anywhere else, and stay still while your finger is on them. Only a touched fader changes a value.
  • Volume ranges: the fader covers min_volume to max_volume, up to 200 % (amplified in software). See Strips.
  • Scribble strips show a label and the volume (or muted, idle, off) on a backlight in the strip's color. A strip whose device or applications are not there goes dark.
  • Mute button with LED.
  • Encoder modes: the encoder sets the balance, fine-tunes the volume, picks the application of an auto strip, or seeks and plays/pauses the media player of the applications. Its LED ring shows what it controls.
  • Home Assistant controls on audio strips: the encoder (or the fader) becomes an entity in Home Assistant, e.g. to dim a light, while the other control keeps the volume. See Encoders.
  • Rec and Solo LEDs as indicators: recording, playing, default or muted. See LEDs.
  • LED meters show the level of each strip, before or after its fader (meter_point), and light their red LED for half a second when the audio clips (a peak at full scale). They are passive: they never wake a device, never light your desktop's microphone indicator, and never switch Bluetooth headphones into headset mode.

items.title: Around it
items.text:
• GUI editor (xtouch-daemon gui): the eight strips as the device shows them right now, editing with errors next to the options, suggestions from the sound server, drag to reorder, undo, a live preview that runs the unsaved changes on the device, and save-and-apply that keeps the comments of the file. See GUI.
  • Command line tools: a device self-test, lists of devices, profiles and applications, a configuration check. See Commands.
  • Robust: survives unplugging or switching off the device and restarts of the sound server and the MQTT broker, and shows everything again when they are back.
  • A proper service: a systemd user service with readiness notification (Type=notify). systemctl --user reload applies a changed configuration without a restart, and the log goes to the journal with levels. Startup and shutdown sequences light the strips up and turn them dark: one after the other, all at once, like a curtain or behind a wave of light. When it stops, it leaves the surface dark.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• Linux with PipeWire and pipewire-pulse (or PulseAudio).
  • pw-record (part of PipeWire) for the meters.
  • Python 3.14.
  • A Behringer X-Touch Extender in MC mode on USB (see Getting started).
  • For Home Assistant strips: an MQTT broker that Home Assistant uses (e.g. the Mosquitto add-on).

items.title: Modules
items.text: Module Role protocol.py The Mackie Control codec: decodes the device's MIDI messages into events, builds the messages that drive it. Pure functions. midi.py Finds the device's sound card in /proc/asound/cards and reads and writes its raw MIDI device without blocking. surface.py Surface: the connection to the device (connects again after it was unplugged), and per Strip what it shows. Sends only what changed, shows everything again after a reconnect, glides the motor faders and keeps them still while touched. audio/model.py AudioState: an immutable snapshot of the outputs, inputs, application streams and defaults. audio/backend.py AudioBackend: the interface the strips use (snapshots, volume, mute, default). audio/pulse.py PulseBackend: one connection to the sound server that follows it by events and carries out the commands. audio/meter.py Meter: audio levels from passive pw-record captures. strips/ The strip controllers: DeviceStrip (and ChoiceStrip for choices), AppGroupStrip, AutoStrip (with AutoAssigner), HomeAssistantStrip, EmptyStrip, and the shared VolumeStrip base. mqtt.py MqttBridge: the connection to the MQTT broker for homeassistant strips. Announces their entities (haad-mqtt-autodiscovery), restores the retained states, passes commands on, publishes availability. mixer.py Mixer: the controllers of one layout of a configuration, fed with every state and every event, and the meter ticker. placement.py place() and Flow: which strip of the configuration each strip of the device shows, for strips that collapse. See Collapsing strips. layouts.py LayoutSwitcher: which layout the device shows, chosen by hand or by the rules (apps, processes, hold); the running processes from /proc. launch.py Launcher: starts the command of a strip's launch detached from the daemon (a transient systemd user service); LaunchButton: when Select launches, and its LED. See Design: launching applications. voip/ VoipProvider: the participants of a voice chat for voip strips, with DemoProvider and BridgeProvider (a client plugin on a Unix socket). mumble.py, integrations/mumble/ The Mumble plugin (C): its sources, building its bundle with CMake, finding it and copying it into Mumble's plugin directory. See Mumble. daemon.py Daemon: the lifecycle (signals, reload, shutdown, systemd notifications) and switching layouts. instance.py The running daemon for other processes: its runtime file (process, configuration file) and where its live view is served. live.py LiveServer: what the device shows right now, for the GUI, over a Unix socket. See Live view. config.py The TOML configuration, validated with pydantic. presets.py The presets (@browsers, @steam-games, ...): named groups of applications for the lists that match them by name, expanded when the configuration is validated. See Design: presets. cli.py, selftest.py, systemd.py The command line, the device self-test, systemd integration (notify, journal log levels, the unit file, controlling the user service). gui/domain/ The configuration editor without a toolkit: the editable document, the options of the models, the look of the strips, suggestions from the sound server, applying a saved file. See GUI. gui/qt/ The widgets of xtouch-daemon gui (the gui extra).

items.title: Data flow
items.text:
1. PulseBackend subscribes to sink, source, sink input and server events. After a burst of events it takes one snapshot (AudioState) and hands it to the mixer.
  2. The Mixer lets the AutoAssigner give the auto strips their applications, then calls update(state) on every controller. A controller shows the state on its Strip: color, LCD lines, LEDs, ring and fader.
  3. The Surface sends only what changed. A fader target starts a glide that moves the motor every 10 ms.
  4. An event from the device goes from the Surface to the Mixer, which hands it to the controller of its strip. A controller turns it into commands to the backend. These run as tasks: nothing blocks the event loop.
  5. The sound server reports the result as a new snapshot, which goes through step 2 again.

A homeassistant strip ignores the snapshots. Its entities work as in haad: Home Assistant sends a command, the entity publishes it as its state (retained), and the copy that comes back from the broker changes the entity; the bridge then tells the strip, which shows it. The device's events go the other way: a fader or encoder publishes its number (a fader moved by hand at most every 100 ms), buttons publish events, which are not retained.

items.title: Lifecycle
items.text:
• Start: the daemon starts the surface, the backend and the mixer as tasks and tells systemd READY=1. The device and the sound server do not need to be there: both are connected (again) when they appear.
  • Reload (SIGHUP): the configuration is read again. A file with errors is logged and the current configuration stays. Otherwise the old mixer is closed, a new one takes over the same surface and backend, and gets the current state right away. systemd learns about it through RELOADING=1 and READY=1.
  • Preview: a configuration of the GUI (see Live preview) takes over like a reload, from memory instead of the file. A reload ends it: the file runs, or the configuration of the file before when the file can't be used.
  • Stop (SIGTERM, SIGINT): the daemon tells systemd STOPPING=1, closes the mixer, turns every strip dark and moves the faders down, waits for the faders (at most 2 s), sends what is still queued and closes the device. A dark surface shows that nothing drives it anymore.
  • Stop, in this order: first everything stops that could show something (the sound server connection, MQTT, the mixer, the device's events), then the strips are reset, and only then the surface closes. A snapshot that arrived during the reset would otherwise paint the strips again.
  • MQTT: the bridge connects (again) on its own, like the backend. On every connect it publishes the discovery configurations, subscribes, and waits for the retained states with a ping on its own sync topic: the broker sends retained messages before later ones. Entities without a retained state then get their defaults. A reload hands the bridge the entities of the new strips; entities of removed strips are removed from Home Assistant (not by a preview, see Live preview). A changed [mqtt] section needs a restart.
  • Status: systemctl --user status xtouch-daemon shows whether the device, the sound server and (with [mqtt]) the broker are connected.

items.title: Design decisions
items.text:
• One snapshot for all strips. Every strip sees the same consistent state, and one connection serves eight strips. The strips derive everything from the snapshot instead of keeping their own copies.
  • Coalesced volume commands. A fader sends many positions per second. A strip sets only the latest one when the previous command finished, and shows the new value at once, so the display does not lag behind the hand.
  • Passive, native captures for the meters. The meters use pw-record with node.passive = true: a capture never wakes a device, never lights the microphone indicator, and never switches Bluetooth headphones into headset mode. They are native PipeWire streams on purpose: WirePlumber 0.5.18 (PipeWire 1.6.10) restores captures of PulseAudio clients (parec, peak detection streams) at 0 % volume, so those would only get silence. state.restore-props = false keeps WirePlumber from saving the captures at all. node.dont-reconnect = true keeps a capture with its device or stream: WirePlumber makes a stream whose target is the default when it is linked follow the default (like PulseAudio), so without it the meter of the default output would show the next default output after Select. pw-record runs under stdbuf -o0 (coreutils): its buffered output comes in blocks of 4096 bytes (64 ms at 8 kHz), so the meters lagged, and two meters of the same audio differed by up to that much. Unbuffered, it writes every cycle of the graph; the daemon takes the peak of every 20 ms.
  • Meter points from the volume. Measured with PipeWire 1.6.10 (a tone into a null sink, the volume and Mute of the test stream and sink set with pw-cli set-param): a playback stream and an input apply their volume and Mute in their own node, in audioconvert's channel mixer, before their output ports, so every capture of them is after both. audioconvert has monitor ports only on nodes with input ports (outputs, capture streams), not on playback streams or inputs, so there is no tap before the volume to link to; node.passive changes only the scheduling. The monitor of an output is before its volume and Mute (monitorVolumes and monitorMute, both untouched, unless monitor.channel-volumes is on). pipewire-pulse turns a PulseAudio volume v into the linear channel volume v³ (50 % is 0.125). So the meters capture what they can and scale it with the volume the sound server tells (meter.scale_of()): pre-fader divides the audio of a stream or input by v³, post-fader multiplies the monitor of an output by it (0 while muted). The audio of a muted stream or input is gone, its pre-fader level with it. The volume news is ahead of the captured audio, so after a change the division uses the loudest of the volumes of the last 0.3 s (GAIN_SETTLE): a fader pulled down must not light the clip LED. Reference: spa/plugins/audioconvert/audioconvert.c (monitor ports in reconfigure_mode() only for SPA_DIRECTION_INPUT; the monitor volume in impl_node_process()).
  • Stall restart. WirePlumber links a passive capture only once and gives up when that fails, e.g. while Bluetooth headphones disappear and streams move. A capture that gets no audio for 3 s while its device or stream plays is started again.
  • The default device follows by name. A strip without device looks up the default in every snapshot, so it follows a switch of the default device, including its meter.
  • One owner per strip. A strip belongs to PipeWire or to Home Assistant, chosen by its type. Mixing both on one fader would make two sources fight over the motor.
  • Availability follows the device. The entities are available while the daemon runs and the device is connected, so Home Assistant greys out controls that would do nothing. A last will covers a crash.
  • haad-mqtt-autodiscovery as a path dependency. The entities are the same as haad's, used from a checkout next to this one (like haad does), which also sets the Python version to 3.14.
  • No volume restore in the daemon. The sound server keeps the volumes. The daemon remembers only the volume of an idle application strip, for its next stream, and only while it runs.

items.title: GUI
items.text:
xtouch-daemon gui is an optional editor for the configuration file, in the subpackage gui and the extra of the same name, like the GUI of openhasp-config-manager. The daemon itself does not import it.

  • Toolkit-free domain, thin widgets. gui/domain decides everything: ConfigDocument holds the file as plain values, validates it with the pydantic models (the same messages as check-config), and saves it. looks() says how each strip appears on the device and faces() whether the preview shows it live or from the file, status whether the device runs the saved file, sources turns sound server snapshots into suggestions, apply() decides between reload, restart and "the daemon does not run". gui/qt only shows that and passes edits back.
  • What applies where. The strips on top show the device (see Live view) and are how a strip is picked: a click, the arrow keys, dragging (Escape cancels) or Ctrl+arrows to move it, a context menu. Below them one tab holds the options of the selected strip and another the global settings ([behavior], [aliases], [mqtt] as "Home Assistant", [device]), so a global setting never looks like one of the selected strip. A strip with unsaved changes shows how it will look (marked with a dot), the others stay live.
  • Strips beyond the device. The preview has the 8 strips of the device, the first 8 of the layout. gui/domain/flow.py says where every strip of the layout is, from the file or from the placement the daemon sends (see Collapsing strips), and whether one more could ever get a place; faces() uses it to show each strip with the strip of the device it is on. qt/strip_list.py lists them all and selects the ones beyond 8, which the Editor allows.
  • Undo instead of questions. History (gui/domain/history.py) keeps the states of the document before every edit, so removing a strip or reverting the file asks nothing and Ctrl+Z brings it back. Typing into one option is one step. Ctrl+Z undoes in the document also while a text field has the focus.
  • Forms from the models. schema.py reads the options of every section and strip type from the pydantic models: the type picks the widget (switch, number, choice, color swatches, list chips, masked secret, file), the attribute docstrings become the help, Field constraints the ranges, and Meanings next to a choice (config.py, e.g. INDICATORS) say what each value does; Presets on a list of names (StreamNames, ProcessNames) makes it suggest the presets of its kind. A new option or strip type needs no GUI code; a test fails for an option without help or a value without a meaning. gui/domain/docs.py holds the "Learn more" links into this site, and a test checks each against the headings of docs/.
  • The comments stay. Saving edits the TOML document with tomlkit: unchanged values keep their place and their comments, and moved strips take theirs along. The file is written in place, so a symlinked configuration stays one. Options that a strip's new type does not have go into a comment of its table (StripDraft.kept), so nothing typed is lost and switching back restores them, also in a later session.
  • The daemon is found, not guessed. xtouch-daemon run writes $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/xtouch-daemon.json (its process id, its configuration file, whether systemd started it) while it runs (instance.py), so the GUI finds it wherever it was started, and a second daemon names the one that has the device. A saved file is reloaded (SIGHUP) only when the daemon reads that file; a changed [device] name or [mqtt] needs a restart, since a reload does not take them. The GUI restarts only the service: systemd.Service (shared with install-service) reads the state of the unit, and installs, starts and restarts it.
  • PyQt6, QtAwesome and qt-themes. The same as openhasp-config-manager, so the tools look and work alike. The wheels carry Qt itself, so uv tool install needs no system packages (GTK 4 through PyGObject needs the system libraries and a compiler), Qt paints the strip preview with QPainter and does drag and drop, and pytest-qt runs the widgets offscreen.
  • One visual system. qt/theme.py holds the design tokens: the colors of the dark and the light theme (text at 4.5:1 or more and the outlines of controls at 3:1 or more on every surface, WCAG 2.2 AA, checked by the tests), a 4 px spacing scale, radii, the height of controls and a type scale relative to the desktop font, and the colors of the device for the preview, the same in both themes. Widgets set style roles (theme.set_role) and take their sizes from the tokens instead of styling themselves. The preview decides what a strip shows (a Face: LCD, ring, LEDs, meter, fader) apart from drawing it.
  • One source of truth: the Editor. qt/editor.py holds the document, its history, its validation and which strip is selected. Views read from it and change the document only through it, so nothing keeps a copy that could go stale. It has two signals:
  • changed(Change) comes once per edit, after the document was validated once.
  • selected(index) comes only when another strip is selected: nothing in the document changed, so nothing is validated and no page is shown again. Only the strip page and the preview follow the selection.
  • Changes say what changed. A Change (gui/domain/changes.py) has a Scope and, for some scopes, a path:
  • VALUE: a value in place; the field that made the change shows it already.
  • STRIPS: strips were added, moved, removed or given another type.
  • SECTION: a section was added or removed.
  • ALIASES, LAYOUTS: the list of aliases, or the layouts.
  • DOCUMENT: anything (undo, redo, revert).
  • FILE: the file was written, so the document is the same. Each page's show_document(change) updates only what that scope touches.
  • Built once, updated in place. The pages build their widgets once, and showing the document loads the values into them (OptionRow.load()); no page is cleared and built again. A part that comes and goes (a section that is absent, the strip form of each type) is a page of a Stack that is sized to its current part, not a widget that is shown and hidden. The strip page builds a StripForm for a strip type the first time it shows one, and keeps it.
  • No layout for what stays the same. Showing the document again, or a live update 20 times a second, changes no geometry when nothing differs:
  • set_text and the tab texts are set only when they differ.
  • theme.set_role restyles only for another role.
  • The list chips stay while their values are the same.
  • The layout tabs are filled again only when the layouts or the edited one change. Icons are kept with their name and color (theme.set_icon), so switching the theme draws them again (theme.refresh_icons) without building a page. The tests count it: selecting a strip changes the geometry of the window once, creates no widget and does not resize the window, and a live update that changes nothing lays out nothing (LayoutPasses in tests/test_gui_qt.py).
  • The options in the order of the device. A strip form lists its options from top to bottom like the strip:
  • what it controls (device, match, profiles, the id of a Home Assistant strip)
  • the encoder and its ring
  • the LCD
  • the meter
  • the Rec, Solo, Mute and Select buttons
  • the fader and the range of the volume
  • the id This is STRIP_OPTION_ORDER in schema.py, apart from the order of the fields in config.py. A test fails for an option without a place in it.

items.title: Live view
items.text:
The GUI shows the strips as the device shows them right now, which only the daemon knows. xtouch-daemon run serves that on the Unix socket $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/xtouch-daemon.sock (mode 0600, next to the runtime file of instance.py) for as long as it runs:

  • Whole states, one JSON line each. A client gets the whole state when it connects and again whenever something changed, checked 20 times a second (live.INTERVAL): the LCD lines and backlight, the LEDs, the ring, where the fader is and whether it is touched, the meter level (falling like on the device, see METER_FALL), whether the device, the sound server and the broker are connected, and the fingerprint() of the configuration in use. A line is about 2 KB; a state rather than changes means a client that connects late or misses one needs nothing else. placement tells which strip of the layout each strip of the device shows (see Collapsing strips). version changes when a line means something else.
  • Requests of the user only. A client may send requests, a line of JSON each: the live preview and {"request": "layout", "layout": "gaming"} (or "+1", "-1") to switch the layout, which xtouch-daemon layout and "Show on the device" in the GUI send (the reply tells whether there is such a layout). The daemon takes them only from processes of its own user (SO_PEERCRED: root can connect to a socket of mode 0600), and a line of at most MAX_REQUEST (1 MiB): a longer one ends the connection. Otherwise the GUI changes the daemon through the configuration file and a reload. The state tells the layout shown and the layouts there are.
  • Never in the way. Clients get only non-blocking writes. One that falls behind by more than MAX_BUFFER is dropped (it can connect again), and a socket that can't be made is logged: the daemon runs on without the live view. The server is not one of the parts of the daemon whose end stops it.
  • Applied or not. The fingerprint is a hash of the whole configuration (secrets included). The GUI compares it with the one of the saved file, so it can say whether the daemon took the file, instead of assuming a reload worked (it keeps the old configuration when the new one has errors or a changed [mqtt]).

The GUI reads the socket with a QLocalSocket, without a thread, and connects again while the daemon runs. Without a daemon it shows what the file would show, and says so.

items.title: Live preview
items.text:
The GUI can make the daemon run the configuration in its editor before it is saved (gui/qt/live_preview.py, the daemon side in Daemon.preview()):

  • The whole text, over the live view. StartPreview carries the TOML text the GUI would save (ConfigDocument.render()). The daemon reads it with parse_config(), the parser of the file, so the errors are the same as those of check-config, and runs it like a reload: a new mixer on the same surface, sound server and broker. The file is never written. A text with errors, or a changed [mqtt] (the bridge would need a new connection), is answered with the reason, and what runs keeps running. The GUI sends 300 ms after the last edit, and only a document without problems.
  • Replies the old GUI ignores, features the new one checks. The daemon answers with lines without version ({"reply": "preview", "ok": ..., "message": ...}), which a GUI from before skips like lines of another version. Snapshots tell preview (the daemon runs a preview, and config is its fingerprint) and features (["preview"]); a daemon from before tells none and ignores requests, so the GUI keeps the switch off for it.
  • Always back to the file. The preview ends with EndPreview, when the connection of its client ends (the window closed or crashed), without a request for PREVIEW_TIMEOUT (10 s; the GUI sends KeepPreview every 3 s, so a window that hangs with its connection open ends it too), and when the file is loaded: on a reload (saving in the GUI sends one), and when the file changes on disk (checked every second during a preview). The client is told why ({"reply": "ended", ...}). The configuration of the file is kept in memory (Daemon.file_config), so a file that became unusable meanwhile does not keep the preview running.
  • One preview at a time. A second client takes it over, and the first one is told: the window someone works in wins over one that was left open.
  • Visible. The status line of systemd ends with "previewing unsaved changes of the GUI", the log tells when a preview starts and ends and why, and the GUI shows a pill.
  • Home Assistant entities survive a preview. A reload removes the entities of removed strips from Home Assistant (an empty retained discovery message), which also deletes them from its entity registry. A preview doesn't: MqttBridge.set_entities(..., preview=True) only stops driving the entities it does not have, which stay in Home Assistant with their retained states, so the file restores them as they were. The next configuration that is no preview removes what it does not have, like a reload; entities that only a preview had also lose the retained state they left on the broker, so a preview leaves nothing behind.
  • Secrets stay with the user. The text carries the secrets of the file. The GUI sends it only to a daemon of its own user (SO_PEERCRED on its end of the socket), and the runtime directory is the user's own ($XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, or a directory of mode 0700 in the temporary directory).
  • Layouts too. A preview is a whole configuration, layouts included: the daemon runs it like a reload, keeps the layout shown if the preview has it, and the layout select in Home Assistant gets the layouts of the preview. "Show on the device" switches to a layout of the preview.

items.title: Layouts
items.text:
A layout is a whole set of strips, so switching one is a reload without reading the file: the daemon closes the Mixer and makes one for the other layout, on the same Surface, backend and MQTT bridge. The strips show the new layout at once, from the last AudioState; the Surface sends only what changed. An overlay of the LCDs (Surface.banner) shows the label of the layout across the strips for switching.banner seconds.

  • Who switches. LayoutSwitcher holds the layout shown. Manual choices (CLI, GUI, Home Assistant's select, the Solo chord) switch at once. The rules are checked after every new AudioState and every 2 s (for processes). They are edge triggered: they switch only when the layout they want changes, so a manual choice stays until then.
  • Remembered. The daemon keeps the layout shown in its state directory (instance.layout_file()), unless a rule put it there (LayoutSwitcher.by_rule), and starts with it. Rules that match at the start still switch, since they start from "wanting" default. Home Assistant's select only takes commands: a retained state (maybe of a rule of the last run) is put right once the bridge is ready, instead of switching.
  • Entities of all layouts. The MQTT bridge keeps the entities of the homeassistant strips of every layout (keep), so automations don't see them come and go on every switch; the layout select belongs to the daemon.
  • VoIP strips. Every voip strip is one strip. The Mixer seats the voip strips of its layout in one VoipSeats (strips/voip.py): a strip with person shows the first participant with one of its names, the others (the group) a page of the remaining participants of the VoipProvider. The assignment is computed once per snapshot of the provider. Strips with the same launch share one LaunchButton, so it starts once. The provider runs in the daemon, not in the mixer, so it stays connected across switches and reloads, and it keeps the volume and mute the strips set for each name (change_volume(), change_muted()), which it sends again when a person comes back: the clients start a participant who joins at 100 %. No voice chat client gives other programs a stream per participant, so the participants come from a plugin in the client (BridgeProvider), not from PipeWire.
  • The Mumble plugin (integrations/mumble/plugin.c) is that plugin for Mumble. Mumble calls its callbacks in its main and audio threads; a thread of its own does the socket and never calls Mumble (Mumble's API calls block until its main thread runs them, which would deadlock the shutdown of the plugin). So the volume and the mute are applied by the plugin itself, to each voice in mumble_onAudioSourceFetched, rather than through Mumble's local volume (which the API can't set). The live view tells the GUI whether a plugin is connected, the names of the participants and who is on which strip of the layout shown (Snapshot.voip).

The design and its research are in Design: layouts.

items.title: Collapsing strips
items.text:
With collapse, the strips of the configuration are not the strips of the device: a layout may have up to 32 strips, and the device shows the first 8 that take a place (see Collapsing strips).

  • A strip of its own for every controller. The Mixer gives each controller a VirtualStrip (surface.py) instead of a strip of the device. It keeps what the controller shows, like a Strip does, and passes it on to the strip of the device it is on (target), if any. Moving a controller is bind(): the new strip of the device shows everything the virtual one keeps, and only what changed is sent; the motor glides to the new value. So nothing of a controller (its auto application, a pending volume or switch) knows where it is, and its index (and with it the default id in Home Assistant) is its place in the configuration.
  • A pure placement. place(collapse, absent) takes the first 8 strips that don't collapse. Flow keeps the state around it in one typed record per strip (_Absence: since when absent, collapsed or not), so the hold time (behavior.collapse_hold) and coming back at once are one rule. The mixer asks it after every state (one placement per state) and every meter tick, for hold times that end without a new state.
  • Not under a finger. The mixer follows touches, held buttons and encoder pushes from the events of the device, and a fader moved without a touch (Strip.held); while any of them is there, Flow.update() is told it is busy and nothing moves. The release places what waited. Events of a dark strip of the device go nowhere.
  • From scratch. A new mixer (a reload, a layout switch, the start) places from scratch with its first state: a strip that has nothing to control collapses at once. Hold times are not carried from one mixer to the next.
  • Meters follow. Only controllers on the device get captures, so a strip that waits or collapsed runs no pw-record.
  • The live view tells the placement (Snapshot.placement, an optional field: an older GUI ignores it, an older daemon does not send it and its strips are where they are configured).

ChoiceStrip (strips/device.py) switches between choices with Select. A press is a _Choosing (the choice, the profile still to switch to, whether the default was asked for): the label shows at once, the card switches first, and once its device is there it becomes the default. A failure goes back to the choice shown before, and a press during a switch goes on from its target. With [mqtt] it has a select in Home Assistant.

The design is in Design: choices and collapsing strips.

items.title: Testing
items.text:
The unit tests run without hardware and without a sound server:

  • the protocol codec and the MIDI parser with captured messages,
  • the raw MIDI device against a FIFO,
  • the surface with a recording send,
  • the strips, the mixer and the daemon with a fake AudioBackend,
  • PulseBackend with a fake pulsectl connection,
  • the meters with a fake pw-record script,
  • the MQTT bridge and the homeassistant strips with an in-memory broker (tests/fake_mqtt.py): retained messages, subscriptions, last wills, lost connections,
  • the live view with a real Unix socket in a short temporary directory: clients that read, that don't read, and that go away, requests of the user, of other users and that are too long, and the live preview through the daemon,
  • the live preview of the GUI against a fake live view (a QLocalServer) that answers like the daemon,
  • the Mumble plugin built with CMake and loaded into a fake Mumble (integrations/mumble/test/fake_mumble.c), which calls its callbacks as a script says, against a real BridgeProvider (skipped without cmake and a C compiler),
  • the GUI domain with configuration files in a temporary directory and a fake systemctl, and the GUI widgets with pytest-qt on the offscreen platform, with a fake sound server and the dialogs answered by the tests.

just coverage fails below 90 % line and branch coverage.

items.title: Commands
items.text:
Command What it does xtouch-daemon run Runs the daemon in the foreground. xtouch-daemon check-config Validates the configuration and lists what each strip does. xtouch-daemon init-config Writes the example configuration. xtouch-daemon list-devices Lists outputs, inputs, and the sound cards with their profiles. xtouch-daemon list-apps Lists the applications that play, and which strip takes each one. xtouch-daemon test Tests the LCDs, LEDs, rings, meters and faders, then shows what happens on the device. xtouch-daemon layout Shows the running daemon's layout, or switches to another one. xtouch-daemon mumble-plugin Shows, builds or installs the Mumble plugin of voip strips. xtouch-daemon install-service Sets the daemon up as a systemd user service. xtouch-daemon gui Edits the configuration in a window.

Every command takes -h/--help. xtouch-daemon -V (--version) shows the version.

-c FILE (--config FILE) selects the configuration file; the default is ~/.config/xtouch-daemon/config.toml.

items.title: run
items.text:
xtouch-daemon run [-c FILE] [-l LEVEL]

Runs the daemon in the foreground. install-service sets it up as a systemd user service instead.

Option Meaning -c, --config FILE The configuration file. -l, --log-level LEVEL debug, info (default), warning or error. debug also logs the messages of the device the daemon doesn't use.

The daemon notes its process and configuration file in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/xtouch-daemon.json while it runs, and serves what the device shows on $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/xtouch-daemon.sock for the GUI. A second daemon does not start: it names the one that runs.

Signals:

Signal Effect SIGHUP Reloads the configuration (systemctl --user reload xtouch-daemon). A file with errors is logged, and the current configuration stays. SIGTERM, SIGINT Stops: the strips go dark from the right and the faders go down.

items.title: check-config
items.text:
xtouch-daemon check-config [-c FILE]

Validates the configuration and shows what each strip does. Without a file at the default path it checks the defaults. Example output:

/home/me/.config/xtouch-daemon/config.toml: valid
  1. 'Speaker' output alsa_output.pci-0000_11_00.4.analog-stereo, select makes it the default (cyan, rec: recording, solo: off)
  2. 'Mic' the default input (red, rec: recording, solo: off)
  3. 'Browser' applications brave, firefox (yellow, rec: recording, solo: off)
  4. 'Living' Home Assistant, entities *.*_living_room_* (yellow)
  5. empty
  6. the next application that plays (white, rec: recording, solo: off)
  ...

A strip with choices lists them, e.g. output: Phones, Speaker or Buds (Select switches), and one with collapse ends with collapses. A strip whose meter shows the level after its fader (meter_point = "post_fader", from the strip, its layout or [behavior], see Meters) says meter post-fader. More than eight strips end with The device shows the first 8 of them that don't collapse.

A file with errors names the place of each one, e.g. strip[3].label: String should have at most 7 characters, and the command fails.

items.title: init-config
items.text:
xtouch-daemon init-config [PATH] [-f]

Writes the example configuration to ~/.config/xtouch-daemon/config.toml, or to PATH. An existing file stays, unless -f (--force) overwrites it.

items.title: list-devices
items.text:
xtouch-daemon list-devices

Lists the outputs and inputs with the node names to use as device, their descriptions, volumes and states; * marks the defaults. Then it lists each sound card by its name and description, with its devices and its profiles (name and description), for card and profile of choices and for profiles; * marks the active ones:

Profiles of alsa_card.pci-0000_11_00.4, Family 17h/19h HD Audio Controller (alsa_output.pci-0000_11_00.4.analog-stereo):
  * output:analog-stereo+input:analog-stereo
      Analog Stereo Output + Analog Stereo Input
    output:iec958-stereo+input:analog-stereo
      Digital Stereo (IEC958) Output + Analog Stereo Input

items.title: list-apps
items.text:
xtouch-daemon list-apps [-c FILE]

Lists the applications that play now: their names (and aliases), the presets they are part of (e.g. Brave (@browsers)), binaries and volumes, and which strip takes each one: an apps strip, an auto strip, "ignored" (behavior.ignore) or no strip. Use the names and binaries, or the presets, for match, ignore and [aliases].

items.title: test
items.text:
xtouch-daemon test [-c FILE] [--no-events]

Lights up everything on the device and moves the faders: every strip lights its LCD in a color, its LEDs, ring and meter, and moves its fader up and down. Then it shows what you do on the device (faders, touches, buttons, encoders), and the messages from the device the daemon doesn't use, until Ctrl+C. --no-events ends after the test.

It takes the name of the device from [device] of the configuration. Stop the daemon first (systemctl --user stop xtouch-daemon): only one program can use the device.

items.title: layout
items.text:
xtouch-daemon layout [NAME | --next | --previous]

Without arguments it prints the layouts of the running daemon and marks the one the device shows:

  default
* gaming
  music

layout gaming switches to the layout gaming, --next and --previous to the one after or before it, in the order of the file (after the last one comes default). The choice stays until a rule starts or stops matching. A layout chosen by hand also comes back after a restart of the daemon (see Switching). It talks to the daemon over its live view socket, so it needs a running daemon; the command fails when there is none, or no layout of that name.

items.title: mumble-plugin
items.text:
xtouch-daemon mumble-plugin [--build] [--install]

The Mumble plugin that gives voip strips the people of your Mumble channel. Without options it tells where the plugin is, whether Mumble is installed, and whether Mumble has the plugin:

Plugin: /usr/share/xtouch-daemon/xtouch-daemon.mumble_plugin
Mumble: installed
In Mumble: /home/me/.local/share/Mumble/Mumble/Plugins/libxtouch-daemon.so
Option Meaning --install Copies the plugin into Mumble's plugin directory (native, else the Flatpak's), replacing an older one; then Mumble needs "Reload plugins". Without a plugin it builds one first. --build Builds the plugin from the sources of a checkout (integrations/mumble, needs cmake and a C compiler) into integrations/mumble/build/. With --install: builds it again first.

A release has the plugin in /usr/share/xtouch-daemon/; a checkout builds it.

items.title: install-service
items.text:
xtouch-daemon install-service [--now] [--remove-override]

Writes the systemd user unit ~/.config/systemd/user/xtouch-daemon.service for the installed xtouch-daemon and reloads systemd. --now also enables and starts it. The unit is Type=notify, reloads with SIGHUP and restarts on failure.

The Arch Linux package installs its unit as /usr/lib/systemd/user/xtouch-daemon.service. Its xtouch-daemon install-service writes no file then: it reloads systemd, and with --now enables and starts that unit. A unit in ~/.config/systemd/user overrides the one of the package (systemd prefers it), e.g. one written before by a checkout; the command says so.

Option Meaning --now Also enable and start the service. --remove-override Only remove ~/.config/systemd/user/xtouch-daemon.service, so the unit of the package is in effect. An enabled service stays enabled, and a running one restarts with the program of the package.

Logs: journalctl --user -u xtouch-daemon -f.

items.title: gui
items.text:
xtouch-daemon gui [-c FILE]

Edits the configuration in a window, and applies it. Needs the gui extra, or the package xtouch-daemon-gui-bin (which has the command xtouch-daemon-gui). See GUI.

items.title: Arch Linux
items.text:
The AUR has two packages, built from the releases:

Package Contents xtouch-daemon-bin The daemon with its own Python 3.14 in /usr/lib/xtouch-daemon, the command xtouch-daemon, the systemd user unit /usr/lib/systemd/user/xtouch-daemon.service and the example configuration /usr/share/xtouch-daemon/config.example.toml. xtouch-daemon-gui-bin The GUI, xtouch-daemon-gui, with a menu entry. It runs on the system's Python and PyQt6, and needs xtouch-daemon-bin of the same version.

Install them with an AUR helper, e.g.:

paru -S xtouch-daemon-bin xtouch-daemon-gui-bin

Then enable the service, see Run it as a service. After an upgrade, restart it (systemctl --user restart xtouch-daemon): it runs the old version until then.

items.title: From the source
items.text:
xtouch-daemon uses haad-mqtt-autodiscovery from a checkout next to its own. Clone both side by side and install with uv:

git clone https://github.com/markusressel/xtouch-daemon
git clone https://github.com/haad-org/haad-mqtt-autodiscovery
uv tool install ./xtouch-daemon

uv installs Python 3.14 if your system does not have it. The command xtouch-daemon is then on your PATH.

For the GUI, install the gui extra instead. It brings Qt along, so it needs no system packages:

uv tool install --force './xtouch-daemon[gui]'

items.title: Set up the device
items.text:
The extender has to be in MC (Mackie Control) mode on USB. Out of the box it may be set to the network interface: then it shows IP: 192.168.001.100 wait... and ignores USB.

  1. Switch it off.
  2. Hold the Select button of strip 1 and switch it on: the setup menu opens.
  3. Set Mode to MC and Interface to USB with the encoders.
  4. Leave the menu (Select of strip 1 again, or switch it off and on).

Connect it over USB. It needs no driver. Your user needs access to its MIDI device in /dev/snd: desktop sessions grant it to the logged-in user. Without a session, add the user to the audio group. See Hardware for details.

items.title: Test the device
items.text:
xtouch-daemon test

Every strip lights its LCD in a color, its LEDs, ring and meter, and moves its fader. Afterwards the command shows what you do on the device: faders, buttons and encoders. Ctrl+C stops it.

Only one program can use the device. Stop the daemon before the test (systemctl --user stop xtouch-daemon), and close DAWs that use it.

items.title: Write a configuration
items.text:
Without a configuration file the daemon uses the example configuration: six auto strips, the default input and the default output. To change it, write the example to ~/.config/xtouch-daemon/config.toml and edit it:

xtouch-daemon init-config     # writes ~/.config/xtouch-daemon/config.toml
xtouch-daemon list-devices    # the names to use for device strips, and the profiles of the sound cards
xtouch-daemon list-apps       # the applications that play now, and which strip takes them
xtouch-daemon check-config    # validates the file and shows what each strip does

Up to eight [[strip]] sections, from the left. For example:

[[strip]]
type = "output"
device = "bluez_output.4C_D7_3A_EA_02_76.1"
label = "Buds"
color = "green"

[[strip]]
type = "apps"
match = ["@voip"]   # Discord, Mumble, TeamSpeak and more, see Presets
label = "VoIP"
color = "white"

[[strip]]
type = "auto"
color = "cyan"

Strips that are not configured are auto strips. Configuration describes every option. xtouch-daemon gui edits the same file in a window, see GUI.

items.title: Run it as a service
items.text:
xtouch-daemon install-service --now

This writes the systemd user unit ~/.config/systemd/user/xtouch-daemon.service, enables it and starts it. From now on it starts with your session. Without --now it only writes the unit.

The Arch Linux package has its own unit, so with it the command writes nothing: it enables and starts the unit of the package. The same without the command:

systemctl --user enable --now xtouch-daemon

A unit in ~/.config/systemd/user (e.g. from an installation from the source) overrides the one of the package. xtouch-daemon install-service --remove-override removes it, so does "Use the packaged unit" in the GUI.

Task Command Apply a changed configuration xtouch-daemon check-config && systemctl --user reload xtouch-daemon Restart (after changing [device] name or [mqtt]) systemctl --user restart xtouch-daemon Stop (e.g. for xtouch-daemon test) systemctl --user stop xtouch-daemon See whether the device, sound server and broker are connected systemctl --user status xtouch-daemon Follow the log journalctl --user -u xtouch-daemon -f

To run it in the foreground instead, e.g. to watch the log while you try something:

xtouch-daemon run -l debug

items.title: GUI
items.text: xtouch-daemon gui edits the configuration file in a window and applies it to the running daemon.

items.title: Install and start
items.text:
On Arch Linux, install the package xtouch-daemon-gui-bin (see Getting started). It uses the system's PyQt6, and starts with xtouch-daemon-gui or "X-Touch Extender" in the menu of the desktop:

xtouch-daemon-gui            # the default configuration file
xtouch-daemon-gui -c FILE    # another one

From a checkout, the GUI needs the gui extra (PyQt6). The wheels bring Qt along, so it needs no system packages:

uv tool install --force './xtouch-daemon[gui]'
xtouch-daemon gui            # the default configuration file
xtouch-daemon gui -c FILE    # another one

Without the extra, xtouch-daemon gui says how to install it.

items.title: The window
items.text:
• The strips on top show the device, laid out and labeled like it: the encoder with its ring of 13 LEDs (Mackie Control lights the middle 11), the LCD (the backlight in the strip's color shines around a dark panel and through its characters and the line between its two lines, as on the device), the meter next to Rec, Solo, Mute and Select, and the fader with its dB scale: the middle of the cap marks the value, -∞ at the bottom, 0 dB at 77 % of the travel (behavior.unity_at). The type of each strip is printed under its LCD.
  • A handle under the strips (the short bar) makes them larger or smaller: drag it down for larger strips, up for more room below. The strips keep their proportions, and the GUI keeps the size for the next start.
  • Above them, the layouts of the file, one tab each (see Layouts): the strips and the "Strip N" tab show the layout picked there. ● marks the one the device shows. + adds a layout, empty or a copy of the one shown, and "Show on the device" switches the running daemon to the layout (as saved, or as in the editor during the live preview).
  • Below them, three tabs: "Strip N" holds the options of the selected strip. "Global settings" holds [behavior], [aliases], [mqtt] (as "Home Assistant"), [switching] (as "Layouts"), [voip] (as "Voice chat") and [device]. "Layout" holds the name, label and rules of the layout shown, with buttons to move it in the order and to remove it. A global setting never looks like an option of the selected strip. "Voice chat" also tells whether Mumble is connected, lists the steps of its setup, and installs the Mumble plugin with "Install Mumble plugin".
  • The footer shows the file, whether the device runs it, the problems, and the buttons Undo, Redo, Revert and "Save and apply".
  • The header has the switch of the live preview, shows the state of the service with buttons to install, start, restart or stop it, which unit it runs (see The service), what the sound server has, the zoom, and a switch between the dark and the light theme.

items.title: The service
items.text:
Next to the state of the service, the header shows which unit systemd uses: "packaged" for the one of the Arch Linux package (/usr/lib/systemd/user/xtouch-daemon.service), or "from" and the program of a unit in ~/.config/systemd/user, which install-service wrote, e.g. for a checkout.

  • Install and start takes the unit of the package when the GUI is the one of the package: it enables and starts it, and writes no file. Any other GUI writes a unit for its own xtouch-daemon to ~/.config/systemd/user.
  • Use the packaged unit shows while a unit in ~/.config/systemd/user overrides the one of the package. It removes that file; an enabled service stays enabled, and a running one restarts with the program of the package.
  • Restart stands out (with a tooltip that names both versions) when the daemon runs another version than the one installed, e.g. after an upgrade of the package: the daemon keeps running the old version until it restarts. This needs a daemon that tells its version (0.1.0 and later), and only counts for the service of the installation the GUI runs from.

items.title: Zoom
items.text:
Ctrl++ (or Ctrl+=) makes the whole window larger, Ctrl+- smaller, Ctrl+0 goes back to 100 %; the zoom button in the header ("100 %") has the levels from 67 % to 300 %. The GUI keeps the zoom for the next start, like the theme.

Qt scales a window only when it opens, so a new zoom opens the window again at the new size: unsaved changes, undo, the selected strip and the page stay. The zoom is on top of a QT_SCALE_FACTOR of the environment.

items.title: Live view and preview
items.text:
While the daemon runs, the strips show what the device shows right now ("Live"), read from the daemon's live view. Without a running daemon they show what the configuration file would show ("File preview"), and the window says so. A daemon that runs while the device is not connected shows "Live · X-Touch-Ext not connected": the strips show what the device will show once it is there.

While the daemon runs with an [mqtt] section, a second pill tells how its connection to Home Assistant is doing: "Home Assistant" while it is connected, otherwise what is wrong, e.g. "Home Assistant · not authorized" or "Home Assistant · refused". Its tooltip has the broker's own words and what to check; a click opens the settings.

The strips are live only while the device shows the layout picked above; the others show what the file would show. An inherit strip shows the strip of the default layout at its place.

A strip with unsaved changes shows how it will look once saved, marked with a dot; the others stay live. Strips after the configured ones are drawn fainter: they are not configured, so they are auto strips.

items.title: Live preview
items.text:
The switch "Live preview" in the header makes the device run the configuration in the editor before it is saved: the device follows every change a moment after it (undo and redo too), and the strips show it live. The file is not written. The switch is off whenever the window opens.

  • While it is on, the pill "Previewing unsaved changes" says that the device runs what is in the editor, not the file. Strips with unsaved changes keep their dot, and are live too.
  • Save and apply makes it the configuration: the daemon loads the saved file, which is what the device shows already. The switch stays on for the next change.
  • Back to the file: turning the switch off, closing the window (it asks about unsaved changes as usual, and says that the device runs them) or "Revert" brings back the saved file. So does a window that crashed: the daemon goes back to the file when the connection of the window ends, or when the window does not answer for 10 seconds. The file also comes back when it changes on disk, or the daemon is reloaded; then the switch goes off and the window says why.
  • What the daemon does not take shows in red under the pills, and the device keeps the version before. A preview can't change [mqtt] (that takes a save and a restart), and a changed [device] name takes effect only with a restart. A configuration with problems is not sent at all: the pill says "Live preview paused" until they are fixed.
  • Layouts are part of it: layouts added, renamed or changed in the editor run on the device as they are. The device stays on the layout it shows (the default one, if the preview does not have it); "Show on the device" switches to the layout being edited, also to one that is not saved yet. The strips of a layout are live only while the device shows it.
  • One window at a time: a second window that turns the live preview on takes it over, and the first one's switch goes off.
  • Home Assistant: strips the preview does not have keep their entities in Home Assistant (with their state; only nothing drives them), so they are as before once the file runs again. Entities of strips only the preview had are removed again when it ends.

The switch is off, and its tooltip says why, while no daemon runs, while the daemon reads another file, and for a daemon from before the live preview (restart it to run the installed version).

items.title: Selecting and moving strips
items.text:
Action Mouse Keyboard Select a strip Click it. Left/Right arrows, Home, End. Move a strip Drag it. The others make room where it goes. Ctrl+Left, Ctrl+Right. Cancel a drag Escape. Remove a strip Context menu, or "Remove" on its tab. Delete. Configure a strip that is not configured Double-click it, or its context menu.

Only configured strips move, to any of the 8 places; the places in between become auto strips. Removing a strip makes its place an auto strip, so the other strips stay where they are. The tab of a strip also has buttons to move it left and right.

The strips on top are the first 8 of the layout. While it has 8 strips or more, or one of them collapses (see Collapsing strips), a row of buttons above them lists every strip with where it is: on a strip of the device ("on 3"), collapsed, or waiting for a place. A click selects it, also a strip beyond the 8. "Add strip" adds an auto strip at the end; it is off, and its tooltip says why, while a new strip could never show (8 strips without collapse before it). While the daemon runs the layout, a strip that collapsed is drawn fainter with its look from the file, and the others show what their strips of the device show. The buttons of voip strips say who is on them ("4 voip: Bob · on 4").

The preview prints the type of each strip under its LCD. A voip strip says which kind it is: "VOIP GROUP" for a strip of the group, the first name of its person for a strip for one person.

items.title: Editing options
items.text:
The forms come from the options of the configuration, so every option has a field. The options of a strip are in the order of the device, from top to bottom: what the strip controls, the encoder, the LCD, the meter, the buttons (Rec, Solo, Mute, Select), the fader and its volume range, and the id last (first for a homeassistant strip, where it is what the strip controls).

  • switches for on/off options, numbers with their ranges, choices, color swatches, lists as chips, masked fields for secrets, and file pickers;
  • the help of each option under its field, with its default and, where the documentation explains more, a "Learn more" link to that section; a button sets the option back to its default;
  • choices as a table, with the devices, the sound cards and the profiles of the card of each line to pick from. While a strip has choices, device and profiles are hidden, and the other way around: a strip has one or the other;
  • for choices, what the chosen value does (e.g. recording for the Rec LED), and each value says it as a tooltip in the list; the type of a strip says what that type controls;
  • the errors next to the options they belong to, with the same messages as xtouch-daemon check-config. The problems button in the footer lists them all; a click opens the page of the problem. An unknown option can be removed from there.

[mqtt] can be added and removed on its page. Above its options, the page shows how the daemon's connection is doing (or that the daemon runs without the section, which it reads only when it starts), and "Test connection" connects once with the settings as they are in the editor, saved or not, and says what is wrong if that fails.

items.title: Changing the type of a strip
items.text:
The buttons above the options of a strip change its type. Options the new type has too stay as they are, e.g. label and color. The others are not lost: the editor keeps them in the strip's table in the file, as a comment the daemon ignores, and switching back to the type restores them. That also works after saving and closing the GUI:

[[strip]]
type = "empty"
# kept from type = "output" (the GUI restores these when the strip is switched back):
# device = "bluez_output.*"
# profiles = [
#   { label = "Phones", profile = "output:analog-stereo+input:analog-stereo" },
#   { label = "Speaker", profile = "output:iec958-stereo+input:analog-stereo" },
# ]

The page of the strip names the options it keeps, and for which type. Restored options look as they did in the file, comments included. A comment edited by hand into something that is no TOML any more stays in the file as it is; the page says so. Ctrl+Z undoes a change of the type with what it kept and restored.

items.title: Suggestions from the sound server
items.text:
The GUI reads the sound server and suggests what it has:

Option Suggestions device The outputs or inputs by node name, with their descriptions; the default is marked. profiles The profiles of the sound cards of those devices; the active one is marked. match, behavior.ignore, apps of a layout The presets (@browsers, ...) first, then the names and binaries of the applications that play. A preset's tooltip tells what it stands for; its chip is outlined. processes of a layout The presets for processes. [aliases] The names of the applications that play. person of a voip strip The people in the voice chat now, as the running daemon tells them.

The refresh button in the header reads the sound server again, e.g. after you started an application. Without a sound server, type the names by hand. The people of the voice chat come from the daemon's live view: without a running daemon (or nobody in the channel), type the names by hand. A voip strip without person is one of the group.

items.title: Undo
items.text:
Every edit can be undone: Ctrl+Z undoes, Ctrl+Shift+Z redoes. That includes removing a strip and reverting the file, so neither asks first. Typing into one option is one step. Ctrl+Z undoes in the document also while a text field has the focus.

Closing the window with unsaved changes asks whether to save them.

items.title: Save and apply
items.text:
"Save and apply" (Ctrl+S) writes the file and reloads the daemon:

  • It saves only a file without problems: the daemon would not take one with problems.
  • Unchanged values keep their place and their comments, and moved strips take theirs along. The file is written in place, so a symlinked configuration stays one.
  • It reloads the running daemon when that reads the saved file: the service, or one started from a terminal or an IDE.
  • A changed [device] name is reloaded, but takes a restart to take effect. A changed [mqtt] section is not reloaded at all. In both cases the window offers "Restart the service" for the service; restart a daemon that runs elsewhere where it runs.
  • It then tells whether the device runs the saved file: "The device runs the saved file", or "The device does not run the saved file yet". If that stays, the daemon did not take the file, and its log says why (journalctl --user -u xtouch-daemon).

"Revert" drops the changes and reads the file again (Undo brings them back).

items.title: The service
items.text:
The service button installs, starts and restarts the systemd user service, the same as xtouch-daemon install-service. It asks before it installs or starts it. While the service runs, "Stop" next to it stops it (systemctl --user stop): it stays enabled, so it starts again with the next session, or with "Start".

A daemon that runs outside systemd (e.g. from a terminal or an IDE) is found too: the header shows "running elsewhere", and saving reloads it. The GUI does not start, restart or stop that one: restart it where it runs.

items.title: Hardware
items.text:
The Behringer X-Touch Extender has 8 strips. Each has a 100 mm motorized, touch-sensitive fader, four buttons with LEDs (Rec, Solo, Mute, Select), an encoder with a push button and an LED ring, an LED meter, and an LCD with two lines of 7 characters and one of 8 backlight colors.

The meter has 8 LEDs: seven for the level (green, then orange) and a red clip LED at the top. Mackie Control sets it in 14 levels, about two per LED (only the 14th lights the clip LED), and the device lets it fall by itself. What the levels mean on an audio strip, and whether they are taken before or after the fader, is in Meters.

xtouch-daemon drives it over USB in its Mackie Control mode, so it acts as the "host" a DAW would be. The device needs no driver: it is a USB class compliant MIDI device.

items.title: Setting up the device
items.text:
The extender has to be in MC mode on USB. Out of the box it may be set to the network interface: then it shows IP: 192.168.001.100 wait... and ignores USB.

  1. Switch it off.
  2. Hold the Select button of strip 1 and switch it on: the setup menu opens.
  3. Set Mode to MC and Interface to USB with the encoders.
  4. Leave the menu (Select of strip 1 again, or switch it off and on).

Check it with xtouch-daemon test: every strip lights its LCD in a color, its LEDs, ring and meter, and moves its fader. Afterwards the command echoes what you do on the device.

items.title: Linux access
items.text:
Linux lists the extender as a sound card (/proc/asound/cards: XTouchExt ... X-Touch-Ext) with the raw MIDI device /dev/snd/midiC<card>D0. xtouch-daemon finds the card by its name ([device] name) and opens that device directly, without ALSA sequencer or JACK.

The user needs read and write access to it. Desktop sessions give it to the logged-in user through the seat (logind). Without a session, add the user to the audio group.

Only one program can have the device open. Stop the daemon before xtouch-daemon test, and close DAWs that use it.

items.title: Motor faders
items.text:
• Touch: while a finger is on a fader, its motor does not follow outside changes. When the fader is let go, it moves to the strip's current value, usually the one that was set last.
  • Only a touched fader sets a value: the device reports a touch about 50-100 ms after the first moves of a quick hand. A move without a touch waits for one for 0.3 s with the motor still: with a touch it was the hand and counts, without one it was the device itself (e.g. its faders going down after it was switched on), and the fader goes back to its value. A fader whose touch sensor failed can't change the volume until it is repaired, or until it is one of the touchless_faders. With touch_required = false, every move of every fader counts.
  • Smooth motion: a fader glides to a new value instead of jumping there. It follows its target like a critically damped spring (no overshoot) that gets there in about 100 ms, starting from where it is, also from where a hand left it. The spring keeps its speed when the target moves on, so a volume dragged in another mixer, which arrives in small steps, becomes one even movement.
  • Arriving: once a fader is there, its value is sent twice more (after 0.15 s and 0.4 s), in case the motor stopped short of it. Stopping the daemon waits for that.
  • Slow moves: the big moves glide three times slower, and stay slow until the fader arrived: a fader that is put away because its strip goes dark (the daemon stops, an application ended, a reload), and the first move after a connect. After a fast move the motor stops a little short of the bottom; a slow one gets there. Tried on the device: neither sending the value again nor a nudge (a little up, then down again) did as well.
  • Startup and shutdown sequences: after a connect the strips light up and their faders come up; when the daemon stops they go dark and their faders go down. By default one after the other, from the left and from the right; [device] startup and shutdown choose others, see Startup and shutdown sequences. The device can't blink a ring and has no brightness levels, so the light effects are steps of on and off.
  • Start: the device can't tell where its faders are. It reports a position only while a finger moves a fader, not after a connect, not on the device query, not after a motor move. So after a connect a fader is assumed at the bottom, where the daemon leaves the faders when it stops, and glides from there. If it was moved while the daemon did not run, its first step jumps from where it really is.
  • Motor noise: slight steps can be heard while a fader moves, more above about 70 %. They come from the device, not from the values sent: a perfectly even 14-bit ramp at 100 Hz sounds the same. The motor control works in small steps (the positions the device reports are multiples of 4, so 12 bits), and the slider has play on its rail: the belt tilts it one way going up and the other way going down, which clicks. Don't grease it: the touch sensing goes through the knob and slider.
  • Fast moves: the device sends many positions per second. Only the latest one is set when the previous command finished, so a slow sound server does not build a queue.

items.title: Protocol
items.text: The Mackie Control protocol; the extender is an MCU XT (model id 0x15). Verified on the device (2026-11-15) unless marked otherwise. n is the strip, 0..7.

items.title: From the device
items.text: Element Message Host query F0 00 00 66 15 01 <7 byte serial> <4 byte challenge> F7, sent on its own after start. The device works without an answer. Fader Pitch bend on channel n: En lsb msb, 14 bits (0x0000..0x3FFF) Fader touch Note 0x68 + n, velocity 7F touched, 00 released Buttons Note on, velocity 7F pressed, 00 released: Rec 0x00 + n, Solo 0x08 + n, Mute 0x10 + n, Select 0x18 + n Encoder turn CC 0x10 + n: 01..3F clockwise, 41..7F counter-clockwise (the low 6 bits are the steps) Encoder push Note 0x20 + n

items.title: To the device
items.text:
Element Message Fader motor Pitch bend, like the fader position Button LEDs Note of the button, velocity 7F on, 01 flashing, 00 off LED ring CC 0x30 + n, value 0x40 (center LED) | mode << 4 (0 dot, 1 boost/cut, 2 wrap, 3 spread) | position 0 (off) or 1..11. The ring has 13 LEDs: the positions light the middle 11, and Mackie Control's center LED (0x40) lights the two at the ends, together. Meter Channel pressure D0, value n << 4 \| level, level 0..14. One more of the 8 LEDs every two levels (1–2 light one, 9–10 five), 11 lights six, 12–13 seven, 14 all eight with the red one at the top. 15 lights none. The device lets every level fall by itself (14 too: there is no overload LED it holds, unlike Mackie Control's 0x0E), so it must be sent again to hold a level. LCD text F0 00 00 66 15 12 <offset> <ASCII> F7, offset line * 56 + n * 7 LCD colors F0 00 00 66 15 72 <8 colors> F7 (a Behringer extension, works in MC mode): 0 black, 1 red, 2 green, 3 yellow, 4 blue, 5 magenta, 6 cyan, 7 white

The codec is in protocol.py: pure functions that decode the device's messages into events and build the messages that drive it.

Messages the daemon does not use are not lost: xtouch-daemon test prints them (unknown message: ...), and the daemon logs them at debug level (xtouch-daemon run -l debug). They show what a device sends that differs from the table above, e.g. a touch that is not the usual note.

See Troubleshooting for problems with the device.

items.title: Home Assistant
items.text: A homeassistant strip belongs to Home Assistant instead of PipeWire: every part of it is an entity there, and automations decide what it does. For example, the fader dims a light, the encoder sets the volume of a speaker in another room, a button toggles a scene. The daemon reaches Home Assistant over MQTT discovery, so it needs the [mqtt] section.

items.title: PipeWire or Home Assistant?
items.text: Each control has one owner. The PipeWire types (output, input, apps, auto) control audio on this computer and need nothing else. A homeassistant strip controls nothing by itself; it only reports what happens on it and shows what Home Assistant sets. In between, an audio strip can hand its fader or its encoder to Home Assistant and keep the other one for the volume, see below. Never both on one control: a fader that both set a PipeWire volume and were moved by Home Assistant would fight over the motor.

items.title: [mqtt]
items.text:
The MQTT broker of Home Assistant, e.g. the Mosquitto add-on. Without homeassistant strips the section is optional; with it, the daemon connects anyway and shows the device in Home Assistant.

Option Default Meaning host required The broker, e.g. "homeassistant.local". port 1883 Its port. username none The user to log in as. password none The password, in the file. password_file none A file that holds the password instead, e.g. one only you can read. ~ is the home directory. Surrounding whitespace is ignored. password_env none An environment variable that holds the password instead, e.g. set with systemctl --user edit xtouch-daemon (Environment=). discovery_prefix "homeassistant" Home Assistant's MQTT discovery prefix. namespace "xtouch" Starts every entity ID (number.xtouch_strip_5_fader) and is part of the topics. Lower case letters, digits, _. device_name "X-Touch Extender" The name of the device in Home Assistant.

Set at most one of password, password_file and password_env. A password file that can't be read, or a variable that is not set, stops the daemon at the start with a message.

[mqtt]
host = "homeassistant.local"
username = "xtouch"
password_file = "~/.config/xtouch-daemon/mqtt-password"

A changed [mqtt] section needs a restart of the daemon (systemctl --user restart xtouch-daemon). Until then, a reload keeps the whole current configuration.

The entities are available in Home Assistant while the daemon runs and the device is connected; otherwise they are greyed out. A last will covers a crash. The daemon connects to the broker again by itself when it was gone.

The GUI shows whether the daemon is connected, and why not (e.g. a wrong password), and its "Test connection" button tries settings before they are saved.

items.title: homeassistant strips
items.text:
Option Default Meaning type required "homeassistant". id "strip_<position>" Part of the entity IDs. Set it to keep the entities (and the automations that use them) when moving the strip. Lower case letters, digits, _, at most 64 characters. Unique among the strips. label none The top line of the LCD until Home Assistant sets one, and the start of the entity names (Strip <position> without it). color "white" The LCD color until Home Assistant sets one. 
[mqtt]
host = "homeassistant.local"
username = "xtouch"
password_env = "XTOUCH_MQTT_PASSWORD"

[[strip]]
type = "homeassistant"
id = "living_room"
label = "Living"
color = "yellow"

items.title: Audio strips with Home Assistant controls
items.text:
An output, input, apps or auto strip with encoder = "homeassistant" or fader = "homeassistant" keeps the volume on the other control and gets these entities of the list below:

Option Entities encoder = "homeassistant" number.<ns>_<id>_encoder, and event.<ns>_<id>_buttons with encoder_pressed, encoder_released. fader = "homeassistant" number.<ns>_<id>_fader, and event.<ns>_<id>_buttons with fader_touched, fader_released.

The LCD, the LEDs and the buttons stay with PipeWire. id names the entities as for homeassistant strips (strip_<position> by default: the position in the list of the file, not on the device, which differs with collapsing strips), and the strip's label starts their names. See Encoders for the details.

[[strip]]
type = "output"
device = "alsa_output.usb-*"
label = "Desk"
id = "desk"
encoder = "homeassistant"    # the fader sets the volume, the encoder dims the desk lamp

items.title: Entities
items.text:
<ns> is mqtt.namespace, <id> the strip's id:

Entity What it is number.<ns>_<id>_fader The fader, 0..100 in steps of 0.1. Setting it moves the motor fader; moving the fader by hand sets it (at most every 100 ms while it moves, and where it was let go). number.<ns>_<id>_encoder The encoder, 0..100. The ring shows it; turning the encoder changes it by behavior.encoder_step per step. number.<ns>_<id>_meter The LED meter, 0..100 %: 0 is dark, 100 lights it fully; the daemon holds the level (the device would let it fall). Its 14 levels are about 7 % each, 100 % lights the red LED at the top too, so e.g. a CPU load or a power ratio goes in as it is. text.<ns>_<id>_top, text.<ns>_<id>_bottom The two lines of the LCD, 7 characters each. select.<ns>_<id>_color The LCD color: off, red, green, yellow, blue, magenta, cyan, white. select.<ns>_<id>_rec_led, _solo_led, _mute_led, _select_led The LEDs of the buttons: off, on or flash. event.<ns>_<id>_buttons What happens on the strip: rec_pressed, rec_released, solo_…, mute_…, select_…, encoder_pressed, encoder_released, fader_touched, fader_released.

A button does not switch its LED: if a button should toggle something, an automation reacts to the event and sets the LED to show the result. Home Assistant keeps what it set last (retained on the broker), so after a restart of the daemon the strips show it again. New entities start with the configured label and color, the fader and encoder at 0 and the LEDs off. While the broker can't be reached, a strip shows its label, offline and its color, and the device does nothing on it.

Entities of a strip that was removed from the configuration are removed from Home Assistant on the next reload. The entities of the strips of every layout stay while another layout is shown.

items.title: Choices
items.text:
With [mqtt], an output or input strip with choices has select.<ns>_<id>_output (select.<ns>_<id>_input): the choice the strip shows, one option per choice, named by its label (or its device; a second choice of the same name gets a number, e.g. Out 2). Choosing one switches to it like Select on the device, profile first; one that isn't there is refused and the select goes back. The select follows the strip, also when the default changes elsewhere.

action: select.select_option
target:
  entity_id: select.xtouch_strip_1_output
data:
  option: Speaker

items.title: Layouts
items.text:
With [mqtt] and more than one layout, the daemon has select.<ns>_layout: the layout the device shows, one option per layout. Choosing one switches to it, like xtouch-daemon layout; the select follows every switch, also by a rule or the Solo chord, and after a restart of the daemon it shows the layout the daemon started with (see Switching), not the one Home Assistant had last. For example, the gaming layout while the PC runs a game in another room's automation:

action: select.select_option
target:
  entity_id: select.xtouch_layout
data:
  option: gaming

items.title: Automations
items.text:
An automation that dims a light with the fader, shows its brightness on the LCD, and toggles it with Mute:

automation:
  - alias: "X-Touch: fader dims the living room"
    mode: queued
    triggers:
      - trigger: state
        entity_id: number.xtouch_living_room_fader
    actions:
      - action: light.turn_on
        target: { entity_id: light.living_room }
        data:
          brightness_pct: "{{ trigger.to_state.state | float | round(0) }}"
      - action: text.set_value
        target: { entity_id: text.xtouch_living_room_bottom }
        data:
          value: "{{ trigger.to_state.state | float | round(0) }}%"

  - alias: "X-Touch: Mute toggles the living room"
    triggers:
      - trigger: state
        entity_id: event.xtouch_living_room_buttons
        attribute: event_type
        to: mute_pressed
    actions:
      - action: light.toggle
        target: { entity_id: light.living_room }

  - alias: "X-Touch: the Mute LED shows the living room light"
    triggers:
      - trigger: state
        entity_id: light.living_room
    actions:
      - action: select.select_option
        target: { entity_id: select.xtouch_living_room_mute_led }
        data:
          option: "{{ 'on' if is_state('light.living_room', 'on') else 'off' }}"

  - alias: "X-Touch: the meter shows the power of the washing machine"
    triggers:
      - trigger: state
        entity_id: sensor.washing_machine_power
    actions:
      - action: number.set_value
        target: { entity_id: number.xtouch_living_room_meter }
        data:
          # 2000 W lights it fully
          value: "{{ [trigger.to_state.state | float(0) / 2000 * 100, 100] | min | round(0) }}"

items.title: haad
items.text:
The same as a haad controller (a sketch: the entity wrappers are haad's, the names depend on your setup):

@haad_controller(registry_name="xtouch_living_room")
class XTouchLivingRoom(HaadController):
    @haad_ha_entity
    def fader(self) -> HANumber:
        return HANumber("number.xtouch_living_room_fader")

    @haad_ha_entity
    def encoder(self) -> HANumber:
