  • TOML: inline tables can't span lines in TOML 1.0 (tomllib), so the example of the first draft did not parse. The docs use [[strip.choices]] tables; a one-line inline table per choice works as well.
  • Select on a choice that is shown but not the default makes it the default first instead of skipping to the next one, like Select on a device strip. Otherwise the LED would be off and the first press would leave the choice shown.
  • A finished default switch ends the pending switch when the command returns, not only when the state shows the new default: a default that the sound server never reports (another program changes it right back) must not pin the strip to the choice.
  • card takes a description too: the Card model got its description (device.description of the card), which list-devices now shows next to the name. The profiles were already listed with name and description.
  • Home Assistant select: its options are the titles of the choices (label, else device); a second choice of the same title gets a number (Out 2), since the options of a select must differ. The entity is created with [mqtt] only and its id is <id>_output or <id>_input after the strip type. It joins the duplicate-id check (Config.entity_strips()), not home_assistant_strips(), so a strip with choices does not need [mqtt].
  • Duplicate labels are allowed and get no warning: the GUI has no warning level yet (only errors).
  • Validation of strips that can never show: the rule "fewer than count - 8 strips with collapse" lets e.g. 8 steady strips followed by a collapsing one through, which could never show. The check is per strip: a strip with 8 steady strips before it never gets a fader. The message names those strips. The limit is 32 places (voip counted count until it was removed). An inherit strip beyond the strips of the default layout is an error too.
  • Collapsed stays collapsed: a strip that collapsed stays so until it is present again, also when it collapsed without a hold (from scratch). Each strip has one typed record (placement._Absence).
  • Deferring under a finger: layouts don't defer their switches (they switch at once), so there was nothing to reuse. The mixer follows the touches, held buttons and encoder pushes from the device's events and the surface's held faders, and Flow waits while any is there; the release places what waited. The meter tick (every 0.1 s) places a hold time that ended without a new state.
  • Without a sound server nothing moves (the absences are unknown); the first state places from scratch.
  • Layout switches and reloads reset the hold timers: a new mixer places from scratch, as the document allowed.
  • Snapshot versioning: the live view never bumps VERSION for new fields; later fields are optional with a default (mqtt_state, layout, ...). placement is the same: None from an older daemon. It holds indexes of Config.all_strips(layout): the TOML list, with inherit resolved and auto strips up to 8. (While a voip strip had count places, these were places, and Config.places() mapped them to the list; both went with count.)
  • absent of apps strips looks at streams only: a paused media player (MPRIS) without a stream does not keep a collapsing strip.
  • auto strips beyond the device take applications too (the assigner fills slots in config order), so an application may go to a waiting auto strip when all on the device are taken.
  • voip strips collapse one by one, so with collapse an empty call takes no faders and the strips of the group that a small one leaves over give theirs up. (First each place of a voip strip with count; since count is gone, each voip strip, see Design: layouts.)
  • C, voip strips: decided first: strip = N named an entry of the list, so a voip strip with count came with all its places, and an inherit without strip took one of them. Superseded: every voip strip is one strip now, so there is nothing special. An inherited voip strip is one of the voip strips of the layout it lands in: with person a fixed strip there, without it a strip of that layout's group.
  • C, the same place: "the same place" is the position in the list, also for another layout. Positions after the strips of that layout are auto strips up to 8; beyond that it is an error.
  • C, state is not shared across layouts: a layout switch builds a new mixer with new controllers (as reloads do); keeping some controllers alive across mixers would mean moving them between VirtualStrips, flows and the auto assigner, and inherited strips never kept their state before either. So an auto strip takes the application that plays at the switch (usually the same one), and a pending choice switch is cancelled with the old strip (StripController.close()), maybe after the profile switched; the new strip shows the default device as it is then. Documented in layouts.md.
  • C, Home Assistant ids: a strip without id that lands on another place than its own gets the id of its own place (strip_<n>), so a referenced homeassistant strip, fader or choices select keeps its entities. The ids of all layouts are one set, so they are registered once. The same strip twice in one layout is the existing duplicate-id error.
  • C, top-level inherit: allowed when it names a layout or strip (a bare one would refer to itself).
  • C, errors are of the whole file: like the other layout checks they are model errors, so the GUI lists them in the problems, not next to the strip; the preview shows such a strip as "?".
  • C, GUI preview by position: the GUI resolves inherit by list position, like the daemon. (While voip strips had count, the daemon went by places, and the two differed after such a strip.)

items.title: Design: launching applications from a strip
items.text:
Status: implemented as described here; how to use it is in Applications and VoIP.

The idea: the Select button of a strip whose application is not there starts it. A "VoIP" strip starts Mumble and connects it to the server, a "Music" strip starts the music player.

items.title: Where Select is free
items.text:
Strip type What Select does without launch launch output, input makes the device the default (select), or nothing not allowed: Select is taken apps nothing allowed auto nothing allowed voip shows the next page of participants (the LED is on while there are several pages) allowed: Select launches while the voice chat is not there, and pages as before while it is homeassistant an event in Home Assistant not allowed: Home Assistant owns the strip and can never send a command empty, inherit nothing / the inherited strip's not allowed / the inherited strip's

Validation is by pydantic: an unknown option on the other types is an error already (extra = "forbid").

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
[[strip]]
type = "apps"
match = ["discord", "webrtc", "teamspeak", "ts3client", "signal", "mumble"]
label = "VoIP"
launch = ["mumble", "mumble://markus@voice.example.org/Gaming"]
  • launch: the program, then its arguments, as a list. It must not be empty, and no part may be empty.
  • A single string is accepted too and split with shlex.split (quotes like a shell, nothing expanded: no ~, $VAR, globs, pipes or &&). Decided for it because a command line is what people copy from a .desktop file or a terminal, and the GUI's list of chips stays the canonical form (it saves a list). The split happens at validation, so check-config and the GUI show the parts.
  • launch_when_running (apps, auto): Select starts the command also while the application runs. For Mumble that is useful: a running Mumble takes the URL and connects (see below), and mumble without a URL brings its window to the front. Not on voip strips, where Select pages while the voice chat is there.

items.title: Mumble URLs
items.text:
From the Mumble documentation:

mumble://[username[:password]@]<address>[:port]/[channelpath][?title=<servername>][&url=<serverurl>]
  • The port defaults to 64738. Special characters of the channel path must be URL-encoded (Gaming%20Night). Subchannels are separated by /. When the channel can't be reached, Mumble stays in the default channel.
  • ?version=1.2.0 was needed only before Mumble 1.2.4. title and url matter only when the link is dropped into the server browser.
  • A password in the URL ends up in the configuration file and in the process list (/proc/*/cmdline is readable by every user). Leave it out and let Mumble remember it, or use a certificate.

A running Mumble accepts the URL too: on Linux, Mumble's main.cpp hands the URL of a second instance over D-Bus (openUrl on info.mumble.mumble, then the legacy net.sourceforge.mumble.mumble) to the running one and exits; without a URL it asks the running one to focus. Only --multiple starts a second client. Verified in the source (src/mumble/main.cpp), not with a real Mumble.

items.title: When an application "runs"
items.text:
Select launches only while none of the strip's applications runs. "Runs" for each type:

Strip type Runs while apps a stream matches match, or a process whose name contains one of the match entries runs, or the program of launch runs auto the strip has an application (it plays, was picked, or its hold time is not over), or the program of launch runs voip the provider reports the voice chat (connected: the Mumble plugin is there, also while nobody talks), or the program of launch runs
  • Processes are matched like the processes rule of layouts (layouts.process_matching()): the names from layouts.running_processes() (the kernel's comm and the file name of the program, in lower case), containing the pattern. So a silent Mumble (no stream) counts as running.
  • The program of launch is the file name of its first part, matched exactly, not as a part: flatpak must not match flatpak-portal, which runs all the time. For ["flatpak", "run", "info.mumble.Mumble"] that is useless (the program is flatpak), so name the application in match (mumble matches the process inside the sandbox).
  • The processes are read every 2 s (mixer.PROCESS_INTERVAL, like the layout rules), only while a strip of the layout has launch.
  • A match entry like signal also counts unrelated processes whose name contains it. The cost is a Select that does nothing; list-apps and ps -e show what runs.

items.title: Starting it
items.text:
• Never through a shell. The list goes to exec as it is.
  • Detached from the daemon's service. With a systemd user manager (its socket $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/systemd/private) and systemd-run in PATH: systemd-run --user --quiet --collect --unit=xtouch-launch-<program>-<random> --property=WorkingDirectory=~ -- argv…. Otherwise a plain process in a session of its own (start_new_session), stdin/stdout/stderr on /dev/null, waited for by a thread so it does not stay a zombie.
  • Deviation from the first idea, systemd-run --scope: a scope runs the command as a child of systemd-run, which is a child of the daemon, with the daemon's environment. The daemon's service starts with default.target, often before the desktop imports WAYLAND_DISPLAY/DISPLAY into the user manager, so a GUI application started from a scope may find no display. A transient service gets the user manager's environment of the moment, is not a child of the daemon (no zombie, survives a restart of the daemon without question), and its output goes to the journal (journalctl --user -u 'xtouch-launch-*'). --collect removes the unit also when it failed.
  • Logging: every start is logged (info, with the command), a program that is not in PATH is a warning (checked before, with shutil.which, so systemd-run does not fail later in the background), an OSError of the start a warning, an exit of the started process with an error code (fallback mode, or systemd-run itself) a warning. A launch that does not show up in 15 s is a warning. Nothing of it stops the daemon.
  • Debounce: no second launch within 5 s (LAUNCH_DEBOUNCE) of the last one while the application is not up yet, so a double press starts it once.
  • Reload: the launch state belongs to the strip and starts anew with a reload or a layout switch; the started application is not affected.

items.title: The Select LED
items.text:
Strip type LED with launch apps, auto flashes while launching (until the application runs, at most 15 s, LAUNCH_TIMEOUT), on while it runs, off otherwise. Without launch it stays off, as before. voip flashes while launching, then as before: on while there are several pages. "On while it runs" would hide the paging, which is the older meaning.

The device flashes the LED itself (Mackie Control Led.FLASH), the daemon sends it once.

items.title: Security
items.text:
• Commands come only from the configuration: the file, or the configuration of a live preview. The live view only accepts clients of the same user (SO_PEERCRED in live.py), who could edit the file anyway. A preview whose launch runs something is no more than that user can do in a shell.
  • Home Assistant and MQTT can never send a command: nothing arriving over MQTT reaches launch, and homeassistant strips can't have it.
  • No Home Assistant button entity for now. A button per strip that runs the configured command would be safe (it runs only the configured command, never one from MQTT), but it lets anyone who can press buttons in Home Assistant start programs on the desktop, also while nobody sits there. Left out until there is a use for it.

items.title: Later
items.text:
• Focus the window when Select is pressed while the application runs. On Wayland there is no portable way (KWin scripts, GNOME extensions, the Sway/Hyprland IPC differ, see Layouts). For Mumble, launch_when_running with launch = ["mumble"] already does it through Mumble's own D-Bus focus.
  • A launch_process option for commands whose program is not the application (flatpak run, gtk-launch), if match turns out not to be enough.
  • A Home Assistant button (see Security).

items.title: Design: layouts
items.text:
Status: implemented as in Phasing; how to use it is in Layouts.

The idea: the configuration holds several layouts, each a set of up to 8 strips. A "default" layout for the desk (outputs, browser, music), a "gaming" layout with the game, the voice chat, the microphone and one strip per participant of the voice channel. Something switches between them: Home Assistant, an application that starts or plays, a button combination on the device, the command line or the GUI.

items.title: What others do
items.text:
Product Unit How it switches Notes Elgato Stream Deck profile, with pages and folders "Smart Profiles": the application in focus picks its profile, matched by executable; leaving it restores the previous profile. A key action switches by hand. (Elgato) Automatic switching is paused while the editor is open. A manual switch by a plugin can disable the automatic one (bug report), a known pain point. Loupedeck / Logitech profile per application, with workspaces and pages "Dynamic mode" (on by default) follows the active application; off, the chosen profile stays. A button switches workspaces. (Loupedeck CT, user guide) Open-source Linux ports match by process name and window title, falling back to a default profile (loupedeckapp). GoXLR Utility (Linux) device and microphone profiles UI, and goxlr-client profiles device load <name> for scripts and hotkeys (wiki) The profile is a whole mixer state; a "load colours only" variant exists. Mackie Control DAWs (Logic, Cubase) banks of 8 channels Bank Left/Right moves by 8 (by the size of the surface group), Channel Left/Right by 1; the last bank is filled up to 8 rather than left half empty (Logic) The model for "more participants than strips". deej one configuration none; the file is reloaded on change (From the project's README, not re-checked.) Voicemeeter settings files, macro buttons macro buttons and the Remote API load a settings file (From memory, not re-checked.) TouchOSC pages (tabs) of one layout a tab bar on the surface, or OSC/MIDI messages (From memory, not re-checked.)

Lessons taken:

  1. One active layout, switched as a whole. Every product swaps the complete set of controls; nobody blends two.
  2. Automatic and manual switching coexist, and the rules for that must be simple. Stream Deck and Loupedeck make the automatic one win whenever the focus changes; a manual choice lasts until the next change. That is the model here too: rules are edge-triggered (see Switching).
  3. Focus is a desktop concept. On Wayland there is no portable way to ask which window has the focus (KWin scripts, GNOME extensions, the Sway/Hyprland IPC all differ). The daemon knows something better for a mixer: which applications play (PipeWire streams), and which processes run (/proc). Focus can come later as a provider of the same rule engine.
  4. A command line to switch (GoXLR) makes every other integration (hotkeys, scripts, desktop launchers) free.
  5. Banks for variable lists (Mackie): a group of strips shows a page of a longer list, and buttons page through it.

items.title: VoIP participants
items.text: The wish: a strip per participant of the voice channel, with the participant's level on the meter and their volume on the fader.

items.title: Can a mixer see the participants?
items.text:
Not through PipeWire. Mumble, TeamSpeak and Discord mix every participant into one playback stream, so pw-dump shows one node per client, never one per participant. The participants are only known inside the client.

Client Participants and talking Local volume per participant From outside on Linux Mumble (1.5) Plugin API: getUsersInChannel, getUserName, mumble_onUserTalkingStateChanged, onUserAdded/Removed Not in the API (requestLocalMute/isUserLocallyMuted mute only). But mumble_onAudioSourceFetched(pcm, …, isSpeech, userID) gets each participant's audio before the mix, may change it (a plugin can apply its own gain) and can measure its peak. The built-in local volume (since 1.3) is not reachable. (MumblePlugin.h) D-Bus net.sourceforge.mumble.mumble: getTalkingUsers, getCurrentUrl, self mute/deaf, transmit mode (DBus.h); mumble rpc the same few commands (RPC docs). No participant list, no per-user volume. Server side (Ice): users and channels, but no talking state and no client-local volume. TeamSpeak 3 ClientQuery (local TCP 25639, API key): clientlist, notifytalkstatuschange, notifycliententerview (client query library) Plugin SDK only: setClientVolumeModifier(connection, client, dB), and the client stores it (forum). No ClientQuery command for it was found. ClientQuery is reachable from another process. TeamSpeak ⅚ has no stable public API (not re-checked). Discord Local RPC (Unix socket discord-ipc-N): GET_SELECTED_VOICE_CHANNEL, SPEAKING_START/STOP events SET_USER_VOICE_SETTINGS (volume 0..200, mute) (Userdoccers) The rpc* scopes are for "approved partners" only (Discord OAuth2); projects use Discord's own StreamKit client id and token endpoint instead, without refresh tokens, and Discord restores the volumes when the app disconnects (Noctalia Discord Voice). Fragile and a ToS gray area.

So per-participant levels need code inside the client (a Mumble plugin, a TeamSpeak plugin). Per-participant volume needs the same (Mumble: the plugin applies its own gain in onAudioSourceFetched; TeamSpeak: setClientVolumeModifier), or Discord's restricted RPC. Participant lists and talking states alone are possible from outside for TeamSpeak (ClientQuery) and Discord (RPC), not for Mumble.

items.title: Recommendation: a pluggable provider, and a bridge
items.text:
graph LR
    Mumble[Mumble + plugin] -- "JSON lines" --> Bridge
    TS[TeamSpeak + plugin] -- "JSON lines" --> Bridge
    Bridge[BridgeProvider<br/>$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/xtouch-daemon-voip.sock] --> Strips[voip strips]
    Demo[DemoProvider] --> Strips
    Later[later: TeamSpeak ClientQuery, Discord RPC] -.-> Strips
  • VoipProvider (src/xtouch_daemon/voip/provider.py): a snapshot of Participants (id, name, talking, muted, volume, level), connected, an on_change callback, set_volume(), set_muted(), run(), and what it can do (Capabilities: volume, mute, levels). The strips show only what the provider can do.
  • BridgeProvider (implemented): the daemon serves a Unix socket; a small plugin inside the VoIP client connects and sends the participants as JSON lines, and gets the commands back. The protocol is the same for every client, so a Mumble plugin and a TeamSpeak plugin both work, and the daemon needs no client libraries. A plugin is a few hundred lines of C (Mumble's API is C) and its own build; it is not part of this phase. To try the protocol by hand, socat - UNIX-CONNECT:$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/xtouch-daemon-voip.sock and a pasted JSON line will do.
  • DemoProvider (implemented): participants from the configuration, with volume and mute kept in memory and a talking pattern, to try layouts and the strips without a VoIP client.
  • Later: TeamSpeakQueryProvider (participants and talking from ClientQuery, no volume), a Mumble plugin speaking the bridge protocol, DiscordRpcProvider only if the scope situation changes.

Bridge protocol (one JSON object per line, UTF-8):

client -> daemon  {"client": "mumble", "participants": [{"id": "12", "name": "Alice", "talking": true,
                   "muted": false, "volume": 100, "level": 0.42}], "capabilities": ["volume", "mute", "levels"]}
daemon -> client  {"set_volume": {"id": "12", "volume": 80}}
daemon -> client  {"set_muted": {"id": "12", "muted": true}}

Every client message is the whole state (like the live view): a client that sends 20 times a second while someone talks needs nothing else. volume is percent (0..200), level the peak since the last message (0..1). One client at a time; a new connection replaces the old one. The socket is mode 0600.

items.title: The Mumble plugin: mute and threads
items.text:
Mute on a voip strip is Mumble's own local mute (requestLocalMute, isUserLocallyMuted of plugin API 1.0), so Mumble shows it and a mute set in Mumble lights the button. The first version had its own mute (gain 0 in mumble_onAudioSourceFetched), because the local mute needs API calls the plugin had no safe place for:

  • Mumble calls the event callbacks in its main thread, and runs every API function there: called from another thread, it is queued to the main thread and the caller waits (Mumble's docs/dev/plugins/MumbleAPI.md, "Multithreading"). A callback that waits for a thread that waits for an API call would wait for itself, and the plugin's mumble_shutdown has to wait for its threads before Mumble unloads the library.
  • No callback comes regularly in the main thread. The talking states come only while someone talks, the users' callbacks only when someone comes or goes; a request of the daemon can wait for neither. The only timers that call plugins are those of positional audio (mumble_initPositionalData every second while no positional plugin is linked), which would make the plugin a positional one in Mumble's settings: rejected.
  • Mumble bounds the wait: a call that doesn't get to run within 800 ms is cancelled and fails with MUMBLE_EC_API_REQUEST_TIMEOUT (C_WRAPPER in src/mumble/API_v_1_x_x.cpp, the same in every release with plugin API 1.0: 1.4.230 to 1.6.870).

So the plugin has two threads: the socket thread never calls the API and only queues the mute requests (a counter per participant); the "Mumble thread" makes the requests and reads the local mute of the participants every 500 ms while the daemon is connected (Mumble has no event for it; the callbacks read it too when they refresh the users). No thread holds the plugin's lock during an API call, so a callback never waits for one. Only mumble_shutdown does: it drops the requests that have not started and waits for a call under way, which can't run then and fails after the 800 ms; the thread makes no call after that. Shutting down takes those 800 ms only if a call was under way at that moment.

While a request is under way the plugin reports the requested mute; when Mumble refuses one, it logs why (api.log) and reports Mumble's mute again, so the button goes back. A locally muted participant who talks has the talking state MUMBLE_TS_TALKING_MUTED, which counts as talking: the backlight shows it, as with the first version's mute. Their level is 0: Mumble does not mix them and fetches none of their audio.

Others' self-mute and deafen are not in the API. Plugin API 1.0 has no function for them (isLocalUserMuted and isLocalUserDeafened are the user's own), getUserComment is the free text of the user, and the talking state MUMBLE_TS_TALKING_MUTED of another user means the local mute: AudioOutputSpeech.cpp sets MutedTalking only for bLocalMute (since 1.6 also for a local volume of 0), while ClientUser::setSelfMute/setSelfDeaf emit muteDeafStateChanged, which the plugin manager doesn't forward (it connects talkingStateChanged only). Someone who muted themselves sends no audio, so they are just passive.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
Backward compatible: today's top-level [[strip]] list is the default layout, named default. A file without [[layout]] behaves exactly as before.

[[strip]]                 # the default layout, as before
type = "output"

[[strip]]
type = "apps"
label = "Browser"
match = ["firefox"]

[switching]               # optional, the defaults shown
hold = 10.0               # seconds a rule must stop matching before its layout goes
chord = [1, 8]            # Solo of strips 1 and 8 together: the next layout ([] for none)
banner = 1.5              # seconds the LCDs show the name of a new layout (0 for none)

[[layout]]
name = "gaming"           # for Home Assistant and the command line: a-z, 0-9, _
label = "Gaming"          # on the banner; by default the name
apps = ["steam_app_", ".exe"]   # rule: one of these applications has a stream (plays or paused)
processes = ["mumble"]          # rule: a process with one of these names runs
priority = 0              # of several matching layouts the highest wins, then the first in the file

[[layout.strip]]
type = "inherit"          # the strip of the default layout at this place

[[layout.strip]]
type = "apps"
label = "Game"
match = ["steam_app_", ".exe"]

[[layout.strip]]
type = "apps"
label = "VoIP"
match = ["mumble"]

[[layout.strip]]
type = "input"

[[layout.strip]]
type = "voip"             # always this person
person = ["Alice", "alice-phone"]

[[layout.strip]]
type = "voip"             # the group: the voip strips without person show the others,
[[layout.strip]]          # Select pages through more
type = "voip"

[voip]
provider = "bridge"       # or "demo"
  • Layouts are a list ([[layout]]), their order is the order of next and of the Home Assistant select.
  • Strips per layout like the top-level ones: up to 8 places, missing ones are auto. type = "inherit" takes the strip of the default layout at its place, so a shared output strip is written once. Inheriting from any layout (inherit = "music") is possible later; one level keeps it obvious.
  • Rules are part of the layout (apps, processes) rather than a separate rule list: a layout says when it applies. priority resolves overlaps.
  • Dynamic strips: every voip strip is one strip. With person it always shows that person; the others form the group of the layout, see VoIP strips: the group and fixed people. Fader: the local volume of the participant, Mute: local mute, meter: the level, the backlight turns talking_color while the participant talks.
  • Validation: names unique and not default; homeassistant ids unique per layout (a strip id used in several layouts is the same entities: one desk lamp, two layouts); voip strips need [voip].

items.title: VoIP strips: the group and fixed people
items.text:
The first version had count = N on a voip strip, which took N places. That made a strip of the file several strips of the device, which inherit, the placement of collapsing strips and the GUI all had to know about, and it gave no way to keep a person on a fader. Layouts were not released yet, so count went without a compatibility path.

[[layout.strip]]
type = "voip"
person = ["Alice", "alice-phone"]   # a fixed strip
label = "Mum"                        # by default the first name

[[layout.strip]]
type = "voip"                        # the group: all voip strips of the layout without person
  • One strip, one place. A voip strip is one strip of the layout like any other. A file with count gets the error "count is gone: write N voip strips; voip strips without person form a group".
  • Fixed strips. person is a name or a list of names of the same person, matched against the participant's name ignoring case and otherwise exactly. Wildcards were left out: names in a voice chat are chosen by people, and a pattern would sooner or later catch somebody else; aliases cover a second device. Of several participants with one of the names, the first in the provider's order is on the strip; the others go to the group, so nobody is hidden. While the person is away the strip shows its label dark with away and its fader parked, like a device that is not there; Select and Mute do nothing then. Select on a fixed strip does not page.
  • The group is every voip strip of the layout without person, in the order of the file, not necessarily next to each other. It shows the participants without a fixed strip, in the provider's order, a page at a time; Select on any of its strips shows the next page (wrapping), the LCD tells the page for 2 s (pg 2/3), and their Select LED is on while there is more than one page, as the Mackie banks do. Strips left over are dark.
  • Collapse: a strip of the group is absent while it has no participant, a fixed strip while its person is away.
  • Validation: a name on two fixed strips of one layout (after inherit) is an error; label is only for fixed strips, since a strip of the group shows the participant's name.
  • launch starts the command once per layout: the voip strips with the same command share one button (LaunchButton), so its debounce and its flashing LED are shared. launch_when_running stays off for voip strips: while the voice chat is there, Select pages.
  • Volume and mute while away. The Mumble plugin keeps them per session (a user who leaves is forgotten; one who comes back gets a new session at 100 %), and the bridge protocol has no notion of names. So the daemon keeps them: VoipProvider remembers the volume and mute the strips set by the participant's name (ignoring case) and sends them again when a participant of that name appears. A mute that changes in the client (Mumble's local mute, set in its window) replaces the kept one, so coming back does not undo it. This is for every participant, not only those of fixed strips: it costs nothing, and someone of the group who reconnects keeps their volume too. It lasts while the daemon runs; the provider survives layout switches and reloads (not a changed [voip]).
  • The live view tells the names of the participants (VoipState.names) and who each strip of the layout shown shows (VoipState.strips). The GUI suggests the names for person, its strip list says who is on which strip, and the preview prints "VOIP GROUP" or the person's name under a voip strip.

items.title: Switching
items.text:
LayoutSwitcher (src/xtouch_daemon/layouts.py) decides; the daemon carries it out.

  • Rules, edge-triggered. Every sound server snapshot and every 2 s (processes) the rules give a wanted layout: the matching layout with the highest priority, else default. When the wanted layout changes, the switcher switches to it. A layout whose rule stops matching stays for hold seconds (a game between two levels, a voice client that restarts). So the automatic switching wins when something happens, and a manual choice stays until then, like Stream Deck and Loupedeck. There is no "lock" mode yet (decided: later, see Phasing).
  • Manual: xtouch-daemon layout gaming (or --next, or without argument: list them), the GUI, the chord on the device, and Home Assistant (select.<ns>_layout). All are the same switch(name, reason).
  • Home Assistant: a select entity with the names of the layouts. The daemon publishes the active layout; a command from Home Assistant switches. Its retained state does not switch (it may be the layout of a rule of the last run): the daemon puts it right once the retained states are in.
  • Remembered across restarts (decided): the daemon keeps the layout it shows in $XDG_STATE_HOME/xtouch-daemon/layout (~/.local/state/xtouch-daemon/layout), unless a rule put it there. A switch by hand and the return of the rules to default write it, a switch by a rule does not. At the start the daemon shows it (if the configuration still has it), and the rules still win: one that matches once the sound server and the processes are known switches to its layout as usual.
  • The device: holding Solo of the chord strips together switches to the next layout. Solo does nothing on audio strips by default; on homeassistant strips the presses are still sent as events.
  • The command channel: the requests of the live view socket (those of the live preview) get one more, {"request": "layout", "layout": "gaming"} (or "+1", "-1"), answered with a reply of kind layout. The snapshot tells layout and layouts, so the GUI and the CLI see the result, and features has layout. Like the preview, the daemon takes it only from its own user (SO_PEERCRED).

items.title: On the device
items.text:
A switch is a reload with another set of strips on the same surface: the old mixer closes, a new one takes the same surface, the sound server state and the MQTT bridge. That gives the transitions for free: the faders glide to their new places, dark strips park their faders. For banner seconds the LCDs show the label of the new layout across the top lines of all 8 strips and the reason (manual, Home Assistant, an application) across the bottom lines; the strips draw underneath and appear when the banner ends. The live view shows the banner as well.

Entities in Home Assistant: the entities of the active layout are announced; those of the other layouts are kept (not removed), so automations and the entity registry don't churn on every switch. Only a reload removes entities no layout has anymore.

items.title: GUI
items.text:
• A layout bar above the strips: one tab per layout (default first), + adds one (a copy of the shown one, or empty). The preview and the strip editor show the layout of the selected tab; everything else (paths strip[3], problems, undo) works as before, for that layout. Problems of other layouts lead to them.
  • A Layout tab next to "Global settings" for the selected layout's own options (name, label, rules, priority), from the pydantic model like every other form, with buttons to move it in the order and to remove it. [switching] and [voip] are sections and get forms for free.
  • The preview is live only for the layout the device shows; another layout is shown from the file, and the bar marks the active one. A button "Show on the device" switches the daemon to the shown layout (the command channel).
  • Phase 2 for the GUI: preview of voip strips with demo participants.

items.title: Phasing
items.text:
Implemented now:

  1. Config: [[layout]], [switching], [voip], strip types inherit and voip, the default layout from [[strip]], validation; check-config shows every layout.
  2. LayoutSwitcher: rules (apps, processes) with priority and hold, manual switching, next.
  3. The daemon: switching, the banner, the chord, the command channel, xtouch-daemon layout, the select entity.
  4. VoipProvider, DemoProvider, BridgeProvider, the voip strip with paging.
  5. GUI: layout bar, layout page, live preview only for the active layout, "Show on the device".

Decided after phase 1: the Solo chord (strips 1 and 8) stays on by default, the daemon remembers the layout itself (see Switching), and Mumble is the first voice chat client with a plugin.

Later:

  • A lock mode: a manual choice that stops the rules until it is unlocked (xtouch-daemon layout --lock, a second option of the Home Assistant select or a switch next to it, a mark in the GUI's layout tabs). Deferred: the edge-triggered rules already leave a manual choice alone until something happens.
  • TeamSpeak (plugin SDK, or ClientQuery without volume). The Mumble plugin is done: integrations/mumble, see Mumble.
  • Window focus as a rule (focused = [...]) through compositor-specific providers (KWin script, Sway/Hyprland IPC).
  • Rules on time of day or on Home Assistant states (an automation can already set the select).
  • Inheriting from other layouts than the default; per-layout [behavior].
  • A GUI preview of voip strips with participants.
  • Remembering the volumes of the voice chat across restarts of the daemon.

items.title: Open questions
items.text: • Answered: a lock mode comes later; the chord is on by default; the daemon remembers the layout; Mumble first.

items.title: Design: presets
items.text:
Status: implemented as described here; how to use it is in Presets.

The idea: common groups of applications (every browser, every voice chat, every game started from Steam) get a name, so nobody has to look up what each application calls its streams and processes. match = ["@browsers"] instead of match = ["brave", "firefox", "chromium", ...].

items.title: Where applications are matched by name
items.text:
Where Matched against Kind match of apps strips the application name (application.name) and binary (application.process.binary) of each stream streams apps of layouts the same streams behavior.ignore (what auto strips never take) the same streams processes of layouts the names of the processes (comm, and the file name of the program) processes "runs" of an apps strip with launch the processes, with the match entries processes the program of launch (all strips, also voip) the processes, the file name of the program exactly none: a command, not a list of names person of voip strips, [aliases] names of people, exact names of applications none

Presets go where the user writes a list of parts of names: the first four rows. The fifth follows from match.

items.title: How a preset is written
items.text:
• @name in the list, next to plain names: match = ["@voip", "my-voice-app"]. An @ never starts the name of an application or process in practice, and TOML needs no quoting beyond the string. A separate option (match_presets = [...]) was the alternative; one list is shorter and works the same in every list.
  • Names are lower case with hyphens: @steam-games.

items.title: What a preset stands for
items.text:
presets.py holds the table: each Preset has a description, the names for lists of streams (streams) and for lists of processes (processes), either of which may be None (not for that kind of list), and a note for the docs.

  • The names are matched like the user's: as parts of the name, ignoring case. A preset is nothing but a list of names, so it can't do anything the user could not write, and list-apps and check-config explain it in the same terms. Exact matching or regular expressions would be a second matching mode for little gain.
  • A preset stands for different names in each kind of list. Streams and processes are named differently: a Proton game plays as Planet Crafter.exe (binary wine64-preloader), but its processes are Wine's, and .exe in a list of processes matches Wine's helpers (explorer.exe, services.exe) and Proton's steam.exe. Steam starts every game through its reaper, which is the reliable process, and has no stream.
  • Errors at validation. An unknown preset lists the known ones. A preset in a list it has no names for says where it can be used. Both are pydantic errors of the option, so check-config and the GUI show them at their place (strip[2].match: ...).

items.title: Expanded when the configuration is validated
items.text:
The models expand presets in an AfterValidator of the list's type (StreamNames, ProcessNames in config.py), so the strips, the layout switcher, the auto assigner and list-apps see plain names and need no changes. The Presets metadata of the type marks the option for the GUI's schema.

The entries as written stay on the model (_WithPresets.written(), a private attribute filled by a wrap validator), for what explains the configuration to people: check-config shows @browsers (firefox, librewolf, ...). The GUI edits the TOML document itself, not the models, so it always shows @browsers and writes it back as it was.

An apps strip with launch counts its applications as running when a process of theirs runs: before presets, the match entries were matched against the processes as they are. Now the plain entries still are, and each preset counts with its names for processes (AppsStripConfig.process_names), so @steam-games counts reaper, not .exe.

items.title: The presets
items.text:
Each is a short list of well-known applications, checked against what they report on a real system where possible (Brave, Mumble and a Proton game on this machine) and against their packages otherwise. Choices:

  • No broad names. steam (the client runs all the time), .exe in processes, chrome in processes (every Electron application runs a chrome_crashpad_handler), element (elementary OS's io.elementary.*), bare zen, jellyfin (the server is a process too), dragon (games). Tests list such names for each preset and fail if one matches them.
  • Streams can't tell who started a game. A Proton game from Steam and a Wine game from Lutris play alike, so the streams of @steam-games and @games are the same: every Windows program under Wine.
  • @games processes: reaper and wineserver. Lutris and Heroic leave no process of their own while a game runs (Lutris's lutris-wrapper names itself only with an optional Python module), so there is no reliable marker for them. wineserver runs while any Windows program runs under Wine or Proton, which on a desktop is mostly games, and a few seconds after it (which switching.hold covers anyway). Native games from Lutris or Heroic are not part of it.
  • Electron. Before Electron 40 every Electron application names its streams "Chromium" (with its own binary), so chromium in @browsers also takes their sounds, e.g. Discord's notifications. Leaving Chromium out of a browser preset would be worse; the docs say it.
  • REAPER. The digital audio workstation's process is reaper too, so @steam-games in processes also matches while it runs. Its users name their games in processes instead; the note of the preset says so.

The docs page lists every preset with its names; a test checks that its table is presets.markdown_table(), so it can't go stale.

items.title: Where presets show
items.text:
• check-config: each preset with what it stands for, in strips and layout rules.
  • list-apps: the presets each application that plays is part of (Brave (@browsers)), to find the right one.
  • The GUI: the options with the Presets metadata suggest the presets of their kind first (a "Presets" section of the menu, the description beside each, what it stands for as the tooltip), then the names of the sound server; a processes list, which had no suggestions, gets the presets for processes. The chip of a preset is outlined instead of filled and has the same tooltip.

items.title: Mumble
items.text:
With the Mumble plugin of xtouch-daemon, voip strips show the people in your Mumble channel, one per strip:

  • the name on the LCD, the backlight in talking_color while they talk, and their voice on the meter;
  • the fader sets their volume for you (0 to 200 %, max_volume of the strip at the top);
  • Mute mutes them for you: it is Mumble's own local mute, so Mumble shows it, and a local mute you set in Mumble lights the button;
  • people who join or leave the channel, and you moving to another channel, show at once.

It needs Mumble 1.4 or later on Linux (x86_64), and a configuration with voip strips. Their [voip] section can be left out: its provider = "bridge" is the default.

items.title: Setup in the GUI
items.text:
The page "Voice chat" of the global settings (the [voip] section) has a box "Mumble":

  1. Click Install Mumble plugin. It copies the plugin into Mumble's plugin directory (~/.local/share/Mumble/Mumble/Plugins, or the one of the Flatpak), replacing an older one. (Without a plugin to install, e.g. in a checkout, the button builds it first; that needs cmake and a C compiler.) Mumble's own installer is not used: with a Mumble that runs, it starts a second instance, which crashed (Mumble 1.5.939).
  2. In Mumble: Settings, Plugins, click Reload plugins (or restart Mumble), tick Enable of "xtouch-daemon", and Apply.
  3. In the GUI: keep provider = "bridge", and give a layout voip strips (see the example below). Save.
  4. Join a channel. The pill of the box says Mumble connected and how many people are in the channel.

The pill shows what the running daemon sees: "waiting for Mumble" while the plugin is not connected (Mumble is not running, or the plugin is not enabled), "not in use" for a daemon without voip strips or a [voip] section.

items.title: Setup on the command line
items.text:
xtouch-daemon mumble-plugin --install

does what the button does (see mumble-plugin); then step 2 above. Without xtouch-daemon's help: in Mumble, Settings, Plugins, Install plugin..., and pick /usr/share/xtouch-daemon/xtouch-daemon.mumble_plugin (a release) or integrations/mumble/build/xtouch-daemon.mumble_plugin (a checkout, after xtouch-daemon mumble-plugin --build).

items.title: A layout for Mumble
items.text:
A layout that comes while Mumble runs, with Alice always on strip 1, four more people on strips 2 to 5 and the rest of the default layout:

[voip]
provider = "bridge"

[[layout]]
name = "mumble"
label = "Mumble"
processes = ["mumble"]

[[layout.strip]]
type = "voip"
person = "Alice"      # her name in Mumble

[[layout.strip]]      # the group: everybody else
type = "voip"
[[layout.strip]]
type = "voip"
[[layout.strip]]
type = "voip"
[[layout.strip]]
type = "voip"

[[layout.strip]]
type = "inherit"

More than four other people: Select on one of the group's strips pages through them. See VoIP strips for the group and the strips for one person, and Layouts for the rules and the other ways to switch.

To start Mumble from the device, give a strip of the default layout launch with a mumble:// URL: Select starts Mumble, which connects to the server and joins the channel, and the layout above comes once Mumble runs. See Launching the application.

items.title: What it does, and what not
items.text:
• Mute is Mumble's "Local Mute" (in the menu of a user): Mute on the strip sets it, Mumble shows it in its window, and setting it in Mumble lights the button. Mumble tells plugins of no change of the local mute, so the plugin looks every half second: a mute set in Mumble reaches the button within about 0.5 s (a press of Mute on the strip shows at once). Should Mumble refuse a mute, the button goes back, and Mumble's log says why ("xtouch-daemon: can't mute ..."). A local mute set from the strip lasts while the person stays; Mumble only stores the ones set in its own menu (for registered users).
  • The volume is the plugin's own. The plugin scales the voice of each person before Mumble mixes it. Mumble's own "Local Volume Adjustment" is separate, and the faders don't show or change it: Mumble's plugin interface has no call for it. The two multiply: a person at 50 % in Mumble and 50 % on the fader is at 25 %.
  • The daemon keeps them for the name. The plugin forgets the volume of someone who leaves; the daemon remembers the volume and the mute the strips set for each name while it runs and sends them again when the person comes back (a mute changed in Mumble meanwhile replaces the one of the strip). A restart of the daemon starts everyone at 100 %.
  • Not their own mute. Whether other people muted or deafened themselves is not in Mumble's plugin interface: it tells their talking state only, and someone who muted themselves sends nothing, so they just don't talk.
  • Your channel only, without you: nobody else's channel, no whispers to other channels.
  • The level on the meter is the voice as it arrives (after the fader), before Mumble's own volume and positional audio. A muted person shows no level (Mumble does not fetch their voice), but the backlight still shows when they talk.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
The plugin (integrations/mumble/plugin.c, plugin API 1.0) connects to the socket of the daemon, $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/xtouch-daemon-voip.sock, and speaks the bridge protocol: the people of the channel on every change and 20 times a second while someone talks (for the levels), and the volume and mute commands back. The plugin's socket thread never calls into Mumble; a second thread makes the calls for the mute, which Mumble runs in its main thread (see the comment at the top of plugin.c). It connects again every 2 seconds while the daemon is not there, so the order in which Mumble and the daemon start does not matter. $XTOUCH_DAEMON_VOIP_SOCKET (in Mumble's environment) points it to another socket.

Flatpak: a Mumble in a Flatpak can't see the socket by default. Let it:

flatpak override --user --filesystem=xdg-run/xtouch-daemon-voip.sock info.mumble.Mumble

items.title: Building it
items.text:
cmake -S integrations/mumble -B integrations/mumble/build
cmake --build integrations/mumble/build

makes libxtouch-daemon.so and the bundle xtouch-daemon.mumble_plugin (the library and a manifest.xml, as Mumble installs plugins), the same as xtouch-daemon mumble-plugin --build. The releases have it built in /usr/share/xtouch-daemon/, CI builds it on every push. The plugin header integrations/mumble/include/MumblePlugin.h is Mumble's (from Mumble 1.5.939, BSD-3-Clause, see include/LICENSE.mumble).

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
"waiting for Mumble" although Mumble runs: check that the plugin is enabled in Mumble's settings (Plugins), and that xtouch-daemon mumble-plugin says "In Mumble: ..." with a path. The daemon logs "Voice chat plugin connected (mumble)" when it connects.

Nobody on the strips: the strips show your channel without you; join a channel with other people. The layout with the voip strips has to be the one shown (xtouch-daemon layout).

Two Mumble clients at once (e.g. a second one with mumble -m -c <other settings file> to test with another user): enable the plugin in one of them only. The daemon keeps the plugin that connected first and refuses the other one; it logs "Refusing another voice chat plugin while one is connected" once.
